abacinate.etymology: LL. abacinatus, p.p. of abacinare; ab off + bacinus a basin.

aback.etymology: Pref. a- + back; AS. on bæc at, on, or toward the back. See Back.

abaft.etymology: Pref. a-on + OE. baft, baften, biaften, AS. beæftan; be by + æftan behind. See After, Aft, By.

abandon.etymology: OF. abandoner, F.abandonner; a (L. ad)+bandon permission, authority, LL. bandum, bannum, public proclamation, interdiction, bannire to proclaim, summon: of Germanic origin; cf. Goth. bandwjan to show by signs, to designate OHG. banproclamation. The word meant to proclaim, put under a ban, put under control; hence, as in OE., to compel, subject, or to leave in the control of another, and hence, to give up. See Ban.

abarticulation.etymology: L. ab + E. articulation : cf. F. abarticulation. See Article.

abase.etymology: F. abaisser, LL. abassare, abbassare ; ad + bassare, fr. bassus low. See Base, a.

abash.etymology: OE. abaissen, abaisshen, abashen, OF.esbahir, F. ébahir, to astonish, fr. L. ex + the interjection bah, expressing astonishment. In OE. somewhat confused with abase. Cf. Finish.

abate.etymology: OF. abatre to beat down, F. abattre, LL. abatere; ab or ad + batere, battere (popular form for L. batuere to beat). Cf. Bate, Batter.

abatis.etymology: F. abatis, abattis, mass of things beaten or cut down, fr. abattre. See Abate.

abattis.etymology: F. abatis, abattis, mass of things beaten or cut down, fr. abattre. See Abate.

abattoir.etymology: F., fr. abattre to beat down. See Abate.

abb.etymology: AS. aweb, ab; pref. a- + web. See Web.

abbacy.etymology: L. abbatia, fr. abbas, abbatis, abbot. See Abbey.

abbess.etymology: OF.abaesse, abeesse, F. abbesse, L. abbatissa, fem. of abbas, abbatis, abbot. See Abbot.

abbey.etymology: OF. abaïe, F. abbaye, L. abbatia, fr. abbas abbot. See Abbot.

abbot.etymology: AS. abbod, abbad, L. abbas, abbatis, Gr. abba father. Cf. Abba, AbbÉ.

abbreviate.etymology: L. abbreviatus, p.p. of abbreviare; ad + breviare to shorten, fr. brevis short. See Abridge.

abdicate.etymology: L. abdicatus, p.p. of abdicare; ab + dicare to proclaim, akin to dicere to say. See Diction.

abdomen.etymology: L. abdomen (a word of uncertain etymol.): cf. F. abdomen.

abduce.etymology: L. abducere to lead away; ab + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Abduct.

abduct.etymology: L. abductus, p.p. of abducere. See Abduce.

abecedarian.etymology: L. abecedarius. A word from the first four letters of the alphabet.

abele.etymology: D. abeel (abeel-boom), OF. abel, aubel, fr. a dim. of L. albus white.

abelmosk.etymology: NL. abelmoschus, fr. Ar. abu-l-misk father of musk, i.e., producing musk. See Musk.

aberrate.etymology: L. aberratus, p.pr. of aberrare; ab + errare to wander. See Err.

aberration.etymology: L. aberratio: cf. F. aberration. See Aberrate.

abet.etymology: OF. abeter; a (L. ad) + beter to bait (as a bear), fr. Icel. beita to set dogs on, to feed, originally, to cause to bite, fr. Icel. bita to bite, hence to bait, to incite. See Bait, Bet.

abeyance.etymology: OF. abeance expectation, longing; a (L. ad) + baer, beer, to gape, to look with open mouth, to expect, F. bayer, LL. badare to gape.

abhor.etymology: L. abhorrere; ab + horrere to bristle, shiver, shudder: cf. F. abhorrer. See Horrid.

abhorrent.etymology: L. abhorens, -rentis, p. pr. of abhorrere.

abide.etymology: AS. abidan; pref. a- (cf. Goth. us-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + bidan to bide. See Bide.

ability.etymology: F. habileté, earlier spelling habilité (with silent h), L. habilitas aptitude, ability, fr. habilis apt. See Able.

abject.etymology: L. abjectus, p. p. of abjicere to throw away; ab + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.

abjure.etymology: L. abjurare to deny upon oath; ab + jurare to swear, fr. jus, juris, right, law; cf. F. abjurer. See Jury.

ablactate.etymology: L. ablactatus, p. p. of ablactare; ab + lactare to suckle, fr. lac milk.

ablation.etymology: L. ablatio, fr. ablatus p. p. of auferre to carry away; ab + latus, p. p. of ferre carry: cf. F. ablation. See Tolerate.

ablative.etymology: F. ablatif, ablative, L. ablativus fr. ablatus. See Ablation.

ablaut.etymology: Ger., off-sound; ab off + laut sound.

able.etymology: OF. habile, L. habilis that may be easily held or managed, apt, skillful, fr. habere to have, hold. Cf. Habile and see Habit.

ablution.etymology: L. ablutio, fr. abluere: cf. F. ablution. See Abluent.

abnegate.etymology: L. abnegatus,p. p. of abnegare; ab + negare to deny. See Deny.

abnormal.etymology: For earlier anormal.F. anormal, LL. anormalus for anomalus, Gr. abnormis. See Anomalous, Abnormous, Anormal.

abode.etymology: OE. abad, abood, fr. abiden to abide. See Abide. For the change of vowel, cf. abode, imp. of abide.

abolish.etymology: F. abolir, L. abolere, aboletum; ab + olere to grow. Cf. Finish.

abolition.etymology: L. abolitio, fr. abolere: cf. F. abolition. See Abolish.

abomasum.etymology: NL., fr. L. ab + omasum (a Celtic word.

abominable.etymology: F. abominable. L. abominalis. See Abominate.

abominate.etymology: L. abominatus, p. p. or abominari to deprecate as ominous, to abhor, to curse; ab + omen a foreboding. See Omen.

abomination.etymology: OE. abominacioun, -cion, F. abominatio. See Abominate.

abort.etymology: L. abortare, fr. abortus, p. p. of aboriri; ab + oriri to rise, to be born. See Orient.

aborticide.etymology: L. abortus + caedere to kill. See Abort.

abortifacient.etymology: L. abortus (see Abort, v.) + faciens, p. pr. of facere to make.

abortion.etymology: L. abortio, fr. aboriri. See Abort.

abortive.etymology: L. abortivus, fr. aboriri. See Abort, v.

abound.etymology: OE. abounden, F. abonder, fr. L. abundare to overflow, abound; ab + unda wave. Cf. Undulate.

about.etymology: OE. aboute, abouten, abuten; AS. abutan, onbutan; on + butan, which is from be by + utan outward, from ut out. See But, Out.

above.etymology: OE. above, aboven, abuffe, AS. abufon; an (or on) on + be by + ufan upward; cf. Goth. uf under. *199. See Over.

abrade.etymology: L. abradere, abrasum, to scrape off; ab + radere to scrape. See Rase, Raze.

abrase.etymology: L. abrasus, p. p. of abradere. See Abrade.

abrasion.etymology: L. abrasio, fr. abradere. See Abrade.

abridge.etymology: OE. abregen, OF. abregier, F. abréger, fr. L. abbreviare; ad + brevis short. See Brief and cf. Abbreviate.

abroach.etymology: OE. abrochen, OF. abrochier. See Broach.

abrogation.etymology: L. abrogatio, fr. abrogare: cf. F. abrogation.

abrupt.etymology: L. abruptus, p. p. of abrumpere to break off; ab + rumpere to break. See Rupture.

abruption.etymology: L. abruptio, fr. abrumpere: cf. F. abruption.

abscess.etymology: L. abscessus a going away, gathering of humors, abscess, fr. abscessus, p. p. of absedere to go away; ab, abs + cedere to go off, retire. See Cede.

abscissa.etymology: L., fem. of abscissus, p. p. of absindere to cut of. See Abscind.

abscond.etymology: L. abscondere to hide; ab, abs + condere to lay up; con + dare (only in comp.) to put. Cf. Do.

absence.etymology: F., fr. L. absentia. See Absent.

absent.etymology: F., fr. absens, absentis, p. pr. of abesse to be away from; ab + esse to be. Cf. Sooth.

absolute.etymology: L. absolutus, p. p. of absolvere: cf. F. absolu. See Absolve.

absolution.etymology: F. absolution, L. absolutio, fr. absolvere to absolve. See Absolve.

absolve.etymology: L. absolvere to set free, to absolve; ab + solvere to loose. See Assoil, Solve.

absorb.etymology: L. absorbere; ab + sorbere to suck in, akin to Gr. absorber.

absorbent.etymology: L. absorbens, p. pr. of absorbere.

absorption.etymology: L. absorptio, fr. absorbere. See Absorb.

abstain.etymology: OE. absteynen, abstenen, OF. astenir, abstenir, F. abstenir, fr. L. abstinere, abstentum, v. t. & v. i., to keep from; ab, abs + tenere to hold. See Tenable.

abstemious.etymology: L. abstemius; ab, abs + root of temetum intoxicating drink.

abstinence.etymology: F. abstinence, L. abstinentia, fr. abstinere. See Abstain.

abstinent.etymology: F. abstinent, L. abstinens, p. pr. of abstinere. See Abstain.

abstract.etymology: L. abstractus, p. p. of abstrahere to draw from, separate; ab, abs + trahere to draw. See Trace.

abstraction.etymology: Cf. F. abstraction. See Abstract, a.

abstruse.etymology: L. abstrusus, p. p. of abstrudere to thrust away, conceal; ab, abs + trudere to thrust; cf. F. abstrus. See Threat.

absurd.etymology: L. absurdus harsh-sounding; ab + (prob) a derivative fr. a root svar to sound; not connected with surd: cf. F. absurde. See Syringe.

abundance.etymology: OE. (h)abudaunce, abundance, F. abundance, F. abondance, L. abundantia, fr. abundare. See Abound.

abundant.etymology: OE. (h)abundant, aboundant, F. abondant, fr. L. abudans, p. pr. of abundare. See Abound.

abuse.etymology: F. abuser; L. abusus, p. p. of abuti to abuse, misuse; ab + uti to use. See Use.

abusive.etymology: Cf. F. abusif, fr. L. abusivus.

abut.etymology: OF. abouter, aboter; cf. F. aboutir, and also abuter; a (L. ad) + OF. boter, buter, to push: cf. F. bout end, and but end, purpose.

aby.etymology: AS. abycgan to pay for; pref. a- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + bycgan to buy. See Buy, and cf. Abide.

abye.etymology: AS. abycgan to pay for; pref. a- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + bycgan to buy. See Buy, and cf. Abide.

abysm.etymology: OF. abisme; F. abime, LL. abyssimus, a superl. of L. abyssus; Gr. Abyss.

acacia.etymology: L. from Gr. ak to be sharp. See Acute.

academic.etymology: L. academicus: cf. F. académigue. See Academy.

academy.etymology: F. académie, L. academia. Cf. Academe.

accede.etymology: L. accedere to approach, accede; ad + cedere to move, yield: cf. F. accédere. See Cede.

accelerate.etymology: L. acceleratus, p. p. of accelerare; ad + celerare to hasten; celer quick. See Celerity.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

accent.etymology: F. accent, L. accentus; ad + cantus a singing, canere to sing. See Cant.

accentor.etymology: L. ad. + cantor singer, canere to sing.

accentuate.etymology: LL. accentuatus, p. p. of accentuare, fr. L. accentus: cf. F. accentuer.

accept.etymology: F. accepter, L. acceptare, freq. of accipere; ad + capere to take; akin to E. heave.

acceptable.etymology: F. acceptable, L. acceptabilis, fr. acceptare.

access.etymology: F. accès, L. accessus, fr. accedere. See Accede.

accessible.etymology: L. accessibilis, fr. accedere: cf. F. accessible. See Accede.

accession.etymology: L. accessio, fr. accedere: cf. F. accession. See Accede.

accessory.etymology: L. accessorius. See Access, and cf. Accessary.

accidence.etymology: A corruption of Eng. accidents, pl. of accident. See Accident, 2.

accident.etymology: F. accident, fr. L. accidens, -dentis, p. pr. of accidere to happen; ad + cadere to fall. See Cadence, Case.

acclaim.etymology: L. acclamare; ad + clamare to cry out. See Claim, Clamor.

acclimate.etymology: F. acclimater; à (l. ad) + climat climate. See Climate.

acclivity.etymology: L. acclivitas, fr. acclivis, acclivus, ascending; ad + clivus a hill, slope, fr. root kli to lean. See Lean.

accolade.etymology: F. accolade, It. accolata, fr. accollare to embrace; L. ad + collum neck.

accommodate.etymology: L. accommodatus, p. p. of accommodare; ad + commodare to make fit, help; con- + modus measure, proportion. See Mode.

roots.meaning: - (cum, signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

accommodation.etymology: From French accommodation , from Latin accommodātiō ( “ adjustment, accommodation, compliance ” ) , from accommodō ( “ adapt, put in order ” ) . Superficially accommodate +‎ -ion . The sense of "lodging" was first attested in 1600.

accompany.etymology: OF. aacompaignier, F. accompagner, to associate with, fr. OF. compaign, compain, companion. See Company.

accomplice.etymology: Ac- (perh. for the article a or for L. ad) + E. complice. See Complice.

accomplish.etymology: OE. acomplissen, OF. accomplir, F. accomplir; L. ad + complere to fill up, complete. See Complete, Finish.

accord.etymology: OE. acord, accord, OF. acort, acorde, F. accord, fr. OF. acorder, F. accorder. See Accord, v. t.

accost.etymology: F. accoster, LL. accostare to bring side by side; L. ad + costa rib, side. See Coast, and cf. Accoast.

accouchement.etymology: F., fr. accoucher to be delivered of a child, to aid in delivery, OF. acouchier orig. to lay down, put to bed, go to bed; L. ad + collocare to lay, put, place. See Collate.

account.etymology: OE. acount, account, accompt, OF. acont, fr. aconter. See Account, v. t., Count, n., 1.

accountant.etymology: Cf. F. accomptant, OF. acontant, p. pr.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting state, office, dignity, profession, or art; as in lordship, friendship, chancellorship, stewardship, horsemanship.

accouter.etymology: F. accouter, OF. accoutrer, accoustrer; à (L. ad) + perh. LL. custor, for custos guardian, sacristan (cf. Custody), or perh. akin to E. guilt.

accoutre.etymology: F. accouter, OF. accoutrer, accoustrer; à (L. ad) + perh. LL. custor, for custos guardian, sacristan (cf. Custody), or perh. akin to E. guilt.

accredit.etymology: F. accréditer; à (L. ad) + crédit credit. See Credit.

accrete.etymology: From L. accretus, p. p. of accrescere to increase.

accretion.etymology: L. accretio, fr. accrescere to increase. Cf. Crescent, Increase, Accrue.

accrue.etymology: See Accrue, n., and cf. Accresce, Accrete.

accumulate.etymology: L. accumulatus, p. p. of accumulare; ad + cumulare to heap. See Cumulate.

accurate.etymology: L. accuratus, p. p. and a., fr. accurare to take care of; ad + curare to take care, cura care. See Cure.

accurse.etymology: OE. acursien, acorsien; pref. a + cursien to curse. See Curse.

accusation.etymology: OF. acusation, F. accusation, L. accusatio, fr. accusare. See Accuse.

accusative.etymology: F. accusatif, L. accusativus (in sense 2), fr. accusare. See Accuse.

accuse.etymology: OF. acuser, F. accuser, L. accusare, to call to account, accuse; ad + causa cause, lawsuit. Cf. Cause.

accuser.etymology: OE. acuser, accusour; cf. OF. acuseor, fr. L. accusator, fr. accusare.

accustom.etymology: OF. acostumer, acustumer, F. accoutumer; à (L. ad) + OF. costume, F. coutume, custom. See Custom.

ace.etymology: OE. as, F. as, fr. L. as, assis, unity, copper coin, the unit of coinage. Cf. As.

acerb.etymology: L. acerbus, fr. acer sharp: cf. F. acerbe. See Acrid.

acerbate.etymology: L. acerbatus, p. p. of acerbare, fr. acerbus.

acerbity.etymology: F. acerbité, L. acerbitas, fr. acerbus. See Acerb.

acerose.etymology: (a) L. acerosus chaffy, fr. acus, gen. aceris, chaff; (b) as if fr. L. acus needle: cf. F. acéreux.

acervate.etymology: L. acervatus, p. p. of acervare to heap up, fr. acervus heap.

acetabulum.etymology: L., a little saucer for vinegar, fr. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.

acetate.etymology: L. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.

acetic.etymology: L. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.

acetous.etymology: L. acetum vinegar, fr. acere to be sour.

roots.meaning: A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.

achieve.etymology: OE. acheven, OF. achever, achiever, F. achever, to finish; à (L. ad) + OF. chief, F. chef, end, head, fr. L. caput head. See Chief.

acicula.etymology: L., a small needle, dimin. of acus needle.

acid.etymology: L. acidus sour, fr. the root ak to be sharp: cf. F. acide. Cf. Acute.

acidify.etymology: L. acidus sour, acid + -fy: cf. F. acidifier.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.
A suffix denoting the art, process, or science, of measuring; as, acidmetry, chlorometry, chronometry.

acidity.etymology: L. acidites, fr. acidus: cf. F. acidité. See Acid.

acidulous.etymology: L. acidulus, dim. of acidus. See Acid.

acipenser.etymology: L., the name of a fish.

acknowledge.etymology: Prob. fr. pref. a- + the verb knowledge. See Knowledge, and ci. Acknow.

acold.etymology: Prob. p. p. of OE. acolen to grow cold or cool, AS. acolian to grow cold; pref. a- (cf. Goth. er-, orig. meaning out) + colian to cool. See Cool.

acorn.etymology: AS. æcern, fr. æcer field, acre; akin to D. aker acorn, Ger. ecker, Icel. akarn, Dan. agern, Goth. akran fruit, akrs field; -- orig. fruit of the field. See Acre.

acoustics.etymology: Names of sciences in -ics, as, acoustics, mathematics, etc., are usually treated as singular. See - ics.

roots.meaning: . A suffix used in forming the names of certain sciences, systems, etc., as acoustics, mathematics, dynamics, statistics, politics, athletics.

acquaint.etymology: OF. acoint. See Acquaint, v. t.

acquaintance.etymology: OE. aqueintance, OF. acointance, fr. acointier. See Acquaint.

acquiesce.etymology: L. acquiescere; ad + quiescere to be quiet, fr. quies rest: cf. F. acquiescer. See Quiet.

acquire.etymology: L. acquirere, acquisitum; ad + quarere to seek for. In OE. was a verb aqueren, fr. the same, through OF. aquerre. See Quest..

acquisition.etymology: L. acquisitio, fr. acquirere: cf. F. acquisition. See Acquire.

acquit.etymology: OE. aquiten, OF. aquiter, F. acquitter; (L. ad) + OF. quiter, F. quitter, to quit. See Quit, and cf. Acquiet.

acquittance.etymology: OF. aquitance, fr. aquiter. See Acquit.

acre.etymology: OE. aker, AS. æcer; akin to OS. accar, OHG. achar, Ger. acker, Icel. akr, Sw. åker, Dan. ager, Goth. akrs, L. ager, Gr. ajra. *2, 206.

acrid.etymology: L. acer sharp; prob. assimilated in form to acid. See Eager.

acrimony.etymology: L. acrimonia, fr. acer, sharp: cf. F. acrimonie.

acrolein.etymology: L. acer sharp + olere to smell.

across.etymology: Pref. a- + cross: cf. F. en croix. See Cross, n.

act.etymology: L. actus, fr. agere to drive, do: cf. F. acte. See Agent.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

action.etymology: OF. action, L. actio, fr. agere to do. See Act.

active.etymology: F. actif, L. activus, fr. agere to act.

actor.etymology: L. actor, fr. agere to act.

actual.etymology: OE. actuel, F. actuel, L. actualis, fr. agere to do, act.

actuary.etymology: L. actuarius copyist, clerk, fr. actus, p. p. of agere to do, act.

actuate.etymology: LL. actuatus, p. p. of actuare, fr. L. actus act.

aculeate.etymology: L. aculeatus, fr. aculeus, dim. of acus needle.

acumen.etymology: L. acumen, fr. acuere to sharpen. Cf. Acute.

acuminate.etymology: L. acuminatus, p. p. of acuminare to sharpen, fr. acumen. See Acumen.

acupressure.etymology: L. acus needle + premere, pressum, to press.

acupuncture.etymology: L. acus needle + punctura a pricking, fr. pungere to prick: cf. F. acuponcture.

acute.etymology: L. acutus, p. p. of acuere to sharpen, fr. a root ak to be sharp. Cf. Ague, Cute, Edge.

adage.etymology: F. adage, fr. L. adagium; ad + the root of L. aio I say.

adagio.etymology: It. adagio; ad (L. ad) at + agio convenience, leisure, ease. See Agio.

adamant.etymology: OE. adamaunt, adamant, diamond, magnet, OF. adamant, L. adamas, adamantis, the hardest metal, fr. Gr. adamare to love, be attached to, the word meant also magnet, as in OF. and LL. See Diamond, Tame.

adapt.etymology: L. adaptare; ad + aptare to fit; cf. F. adapter. See Apt, Adept.

add.etymology: L. addere; ad + dare to give, put. Cf. Date, Do.

roots.meaning: An adjective suffix now usually in a passive sense; able to be; fit to be; expressing capacity or worthiness in a passive sense; as, movable, able to be moved; amendable, able to be amended; blamable, fit to be blamed; salable.

addict.etymology: L. addictus, p. p. of addicere to adjudge, devote; ad + dicere to say. See Diction.

addition.etymology: F. addition, L. additio, fr. addere to add.

address.etymology: OE. adressen to raise erect, adorn, OF. adrecier, to straighten, address, F. adresser, fr. à (L. ad) + OF. drecier, F. dresser, to straighten, arrange. See Dress, v.

adduce.etymology: L. adducere, adductum, to lead or bring to; ad + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Adduct.

adducent.etymology: L. addunces, p. pr. of adducere.

adduct.etymology: L. adductus, p. p. of adducere. See Adduce.

roots.meaning: Combining forms of the Greek word for gland; -- used in words relating to the structure, diseases, etc., of the glands.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

adept.etymology: L. adeptus obtained (sc. artem), adipsci to arrive ad + apisci to pursue. See Apt, and cf. Adapt.

adequate.etymology: L. adaequatus, p. p. of adaequare to make equal to; ad + aequare to make equal, aequus equal. See Equal.

adhere.etymology: L. adhaerere, adhaesum; ad + haerere to stick: cf. F. adhérer. See Aghast.

adherent.etymology: L. adhaerens, -entis, p. pr.: cf. F. adhérent.

adhesion.etymology: L. adhaesio, fr. adhaerere: cf. F. adhésion.

adieu.etymology: OE. also adew, adewe, adue, F. dieu, fr. L. ad to + deus God.

adit.etymology: L. aditus, fr. adire, , to go to; ad + ire to go.

adjacent.etymology: L. adjacens, -centis, p. pr. of adjacere to lie near; ad + jac to lie: cf. F. adjacent.

adjoin.etymology: OE. ajoinen, OF. ajoindre, F. adjoindre, fr. L. adjungere; ad + jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Adjunct.

adjourn.etymology: OE. ajornen, OF. ajoiner, ajurner, F. ajourner; OF. a (L. ad) + jor, jur, jorn, F. jour, day, fr. L. diurnus belonging to the day, fr. dies day. Cf. Journal, Journey.

adjournment.etymology: Cf. f. adjournement, OF. ajornement. See Adjourn.

adjudge.etymology: OE. ajugen, OF. ajugier, fr. L. adjudicare; ad + judicare to judge. See Judge, and cf. Adjudicate.

adjudicate.etymology: L. adjudicatus, p. p. of adjudicare. See Adjudge.

adjunct.etymology: L. adjunctus, p. p. of adjungere. See Adjoin.

adjunction.etymology: L. adjunctio, fr. adjungere: cf. F. adjonction, and see Adjunct.

adjunctive.etymology: L. adjunctivus, fr. adjungere. See Adjunct.

adjuration.etymology: L. adjuratio, fr. adjurare: cf. F. adjuration. See Adjure.

adjure.etymology: L. adjurare, adjurdium, to swear to; later, to adjure: cf. F. adjurer. See Jury.

adjust.etymology: OF. ajuster, ajoster (whence F. ajouter to add), LL. adjuxtare to fit; fr. L. ad + juxta near; confused later with L. ad and justus just, right, whence F. ajuster to adjust. See Just, v. t. and cf. Adjute.

adjutant.etymology: L. adjutans, p. pr. of adjutare to help. See Aid.

adjuvant.etymology: L. adjuvans, p. pr. of adjuvare to aid: cf. F. adjuvant. See Aid.

admeasure.etymology: Cf. OF. amesurer, LL. admensurare. See Measure.

administer.etymology: OE. aministren, OF. aministrer, F. administer, fr. L. administrare; ad + ministrare to serve. See Minister.

administrate.etymology: L. administratus, p. p. of administrare.

administration.etymology: OE. administracioun, L. administratio: cf. F. administration.

admiral.etymology: OE. amiral, admiral, OF. amiral, ultimately fr. Ar. amir-al-bahr commander of the sea; Ar. amir is commander, al is the Ar. article, and amir-al, heard in different titles, was taken as one word. Early forms of the word show confusion with L. admirabilis admirable, fr. admirari to admire. It is said to have been introduced into Europe by the Genoese or Venetians, in the 12th or 13th century. Cf. Ameer, Emir.

admiralty.etymology: F. amirauté, for an older amiralté, office of admiral, fr. LL. admiralitas. See Admiral.

admiration.etymology: F., fr. L. admiratio. See Admire.

admire.etymology: F. admirer, fr. L. admirari; ad + mirari to wonder, for smirari, akin to Gr. smi, and E. smile.

admissible.etymology: F. admissible, LL. admissibilis. See Admit.

admission.etymology: L. admissio: cf. F. admission. See Admit.

admit.etymology: OE. amitten, L. admittere, admissum; ad + mittere to send: cf. F. admettre, OF. admettre, OF. ametre. See Missile.

admix.etymology: Pref. ad- + mix: cf. L. admixtus, p. p. of admiscere. See Mix.

roots.meaning: As a prefix ad- assumes the forms ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, assimilating the d with the first letter of the word to which ad- is prefixed. It remains unchanged before vowels, and before d, h, j, m, v. Examples: adduce, adhere, adjacent, admit, advent, accord, affect, aggregate, allude, annex, appear, etc. It becomes ac- before qu, as in acquiesce.

admixture.etymology: L. admiscere, admixtum, to admix; ad + miscere to mix. See Mix.

admonish.etymology: OE. amonesten, OF. amonester, F. admonester, fr. a supposed LL. admonesstrare, fr. L. admonere to remind, warn; ad + monere to warn. See Monition.

admonition.etymology: OE. amonicioun, OF. amonition, F. admonition, fr. L. admonitio, fr. admonere. See Admonish.

adnate.etymology: L. adnatus, p. p. of adnasci. See Adnascent, and cf. Agnate.

roots.meaning: As a prefix ad- assumes the forms ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, assimilating the d with the first letter of the word to which ad- is prefixed. It remains unchanged before vowels, and before d, h, j, m, v. Examples: adduce, adhere, adjacent, admit, advent, accord, affect, aggregate, allude, annex, appear, etc. It becomes ac- before qu, as in acquiesce.

ado.etymology: OE. at do, northern form for to do. Cf. Affair.

adolescent.etymology: L. adolescens, p. pr. of adolescere to grow up to; ad + the inchoative olescere to grow: cf. F. adolescent. See Adult.

adopt.etymology: L. adoptare; ad + optare to choose, desire: cf. F. adopter. See Option.

adoption.etymology: L. adoptio, allied to adoptare to adopt: cf. F. adoption.

adorable.etymology: L. adorabilis, fr. adorare: cf. F. adorable.

adoration.etymology: L. adoratio, fr. adorare: cf. F. adoration.

adore.etymology: OE. aouren, anouren, adoren, OF. aorer, adorer, F. adorer, fr. L. adorare; ad + orare to speak, pray, os, oris, mouth. In OE. confused with honor, the French prefix a- being confused with OE. a, an, on. See Oral.

adorn.etymology: OE. aournen, anournen, adornen, OF. aorner, fr. L. aaornare; ad + ornare to furnish, embellish. See Adore, Ornate.

roots.meaning: As a prefix ad- assumes the forms ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, assimilating the d with the first letter of the word to which ad- is prefixed. It remains unchanged before vowels, and before d, h, j, m, v. Examples: adduce, adhere, adjacent, admit, advent, accord, affect, aggregate, allude, annex, appear, etc. It becomes ac- before qu, as in acquiesce.

adriatic.etymology: L. Adriaticus, Hadriaticus, fr. Adria or Hadria, a town of the Veneti.

adroit.etymology: F. adroit; à (L. ad) = droit straight, right, fr. L. directus, p. p. of dirigere. See Direct.

adscititious.etymology: L. adscitus, p. p. of adsciscere, asciscere, to take knowingly; ad + sciscere to seek to know, approve, scire to know.

adscript.etymology: L. adscriptus, p. p. of adscribere to enroll. See Ascribe.

adulate.etymology: L. adulatus, p. p. of adulari.

adulation.etymology: F. adulation, fr. L. adulatio, fr. adulari, adulatum, to flatter.

adulator.etymology: L., fr. adulari: cf. F. adulateur.

adulatory.etymology: L. adulatorius, fr. adulari: cf. OF. adulatoire.

adult.etymology: L. adultus, p. p. of adolescere, akin to alere to nourish: cf. F. adulte. See Adolescent, Old.

adulterant.etymology: L. adulterans, p. pr. of adulterare.

adulterate.etymology: L. adulteratus, p. p. of adulterare, fr. adulter adulterer, prob. fr. ad + alter other, properly one who approaches another on account of unlawful love. Cf. Advoutry.

adulterer.etymology: Formed fr. the verb adulter, with the E. ending -er. See Advoutrer.

adulteress.etymology: Fem. from L. adulter. Cf. Advoutress.

adumbrate.etymology: L. adumbratus, p. p. of adumbrare; ad + umbrare to shade; umbra shadow.

adust.etymology: L. adustus, p. p. of adurere: cf. F. aduste.

advance.etymology: OE. avancen, avauncen, F. avancer, fr. a supposed LL. abantiare; ab + ante (F. avant) before. The spelling with d was a mistake, a- being supposed to be fr. L. ad. See Avaunt.

advancement.etymology: OE. avancement, F. avancement. See Advance, v. t.

advantage.etymology: OE. avantage, avauntage, F. avantage, fr. avant before. See Advance, and cf. Vantage.

advent.etymology: L. adventus, fr. advenire, adventum: cf. F. avent. See Advene.

adventure.etymology: OE. aventure, aunter, anter, F. aventure, fr. LL. adventura, fr. L. advenire, adventum, to arrive, which in the Romance languages took the sense of "to happen, befall." See Advene.

adventurous.etymology: OE. aventurous, aunterous, OF. aventuros, F. aventureux, fr. aventure. See Adventure, n.

adverb.etymology: L. adverbium; ad + verbum word, verb: cf. F. adverbe.

adversary.etymology: OE. adversarie, direct fr. the Latin, and adversaire, fr. OF. adversier, aversier, fr. L. adversarius (a.) turned toward, (n.) an adversary. See Adverse.

adverse.etymology: OE. advers, OF. avers, advers, fr. L. adversus, p. p. advertere to turn to. See Advert.

adversity.etymology: OE. adversite, F. adversité, fr. L. adversitas.

advert.etymology: L. advertere, v. t., to turn to; ad + vertere to turn: cf. F. avertir. See Advertise.

advertence.etymology: OF. advertence, avertence, LL. advertentia, fr. L. advertens. See Advertent.

advertency.etymology: OF. advertence, avertence, LL. advertentia, fr. L. advertens. See Advertent.

advertent.etymology: L. advertens, -entis, p. pr. of advertere. See Advert.

advertise.etymology: F. avertir, formerly also spelt advertir, to warn, give notice to, L. advertere to turn to. The ending was probably influenced by the noun advertisement. See Advert.

advertisement.etymology: F.avertisement, formerly also spelled advertissement, a warning, giving notice, fr. avertir.

advice.etymology: OE. avis, F. avis; + OF. vis, fr. L. visum seemed, seen; really p. p. of videre to see, so that vis meant that which has seemed best. See Vision, and cf. Avise, Advise.

advise.etymology: OE. avisen to perceive, consider, inform, F. aviser, fr. LL. advisare. advisare; ad + visare, fr. L. videre, visum, to see. See Advice, and cf. Avise.

advisement.etymology: OE. avisement, F. avisement, fr. aviser. See Advise, and cf. Avisement.

advocacy.etymology: OF. advocatie, LL. advocatia. See Advocate.

advocate.etymology: OE. avocat, avocet, OF. avocat, fr. L. advocatus, one summoned or called to another; properly the p. p. of advocare to call to, call to one's aid; ad + vocare to call. See Advowee, Avowee, Vocal.

advowson.etymology: OE. avoweisoun, OF. avoëson, fr. L. advocatio. Cf. Advocation.

adz.etymology: OE. adese, adis, adse, AS. adesa, adese, ax, hatchet.

adze.etymology: OE. adese, adis, adse, AS. adesa, adese, ax, hatchet.

aeneid.etymology: L. Aeneis, Aeneidis, or -dos: cf. F. .

aeon.etymology: L. aeon, fr. Gr. a'iwn space or period of time, lifetime, age; akin to L. aevum. See Age.

aerate.etymology: Cf. F. aérer. See Air,v. t.

aerie.etymology: OE. aire, eire, air, nest, also origin, descent, OF. aire, LL. area, aera, nest of a bird of prey, perh. fr. L. area an open space (for birds of prey like to build their nests on flat and open spaces on the top of high rocks). Cf. Area.

aeriferous.etymology: L. aër air + -ferous: cf. F. aérifère.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

aeriform.etymology: L. aër air + -form: cf. F. aériforme.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

aestival.etymology: L. aestivalis, aestivus, fr. aestas summer.

afar.etymology: Pref. a-.(for on or of) + far.

afeard.etymology: OE. afered, AS. af, p. p. of af to frighten; a- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + fran to frighten. See Fear.

affable.etymology: F. affable, L. affabilis, fr. affari to speak to; ad + fari to speak. See Fable.

affair.etymology: OE. afere, affere, OF. afaire, F. affaire, fr. a faire to do; L.. ad + facere to do. See Fact, and cf. Ado.

affect.etymology: L. affectus, p. p. of afficere to affect by active agency; ad + facere to make: cf. F. affectere, L. affectare, freq. of afficere. See Fact.

affection.etymology: F. affection, L. affectio, fr. afficere. See Affect.

afferent.etymology: L. afferens, p. pr. of afferre; ad + ferre to bear.

affiance.etymology: OE. afiaunce trust, confidence, OF. afiance, fr. afier to trust, fr. LL. affidare to trust; ad + fidare to trust, fr. L. fides faith. See Faith, and cf. Affidavit, Affy, Confidence.

affiant.etymology: From p. pr. of OF. afier, LL. affidare. See Affidavit.

affidavit.etymology: LL. affidavit he has made oath, perfect tense of affidare. See Affiance, Affy.

affiliate.etymology: LL. adfiliare, affiliare, to adopt as son; ad + filius son: cf. F. affilier.

affine.etymology: F. affiner to refine; (L. ad) + fin fine. See Fine.

affined.etymology: OF. afiné related, p. p., fr. LL. affinare to join, fr. L. affinis neighboring, related to; ad + finis boundary, limit.

affinity.etymology: OF. afinité, F. affinité, L. affinites, fr. affinis. See Affined.

affirm.etymology: OE. affermen, OF. afermer, F. affirmer, affermir, fr. L. affirmare; ad + firmare to make firm, firmus firm. See Firm.

affix.etymology: LL. affixare, L. affixus, p. p. of affigere to fasten to; ad + figere to fasten: cf. OE. affichen, F. afficher, ultimately fr. L. affigere. See Fix.

afflict.etymology: L. afflictus, p. p. of affigere to cast down, deject; ad + fligere to strike: cf. OF. aflit, afflict, p. p. Cf. Flagellate.

affliction.etymology: F. affliction, L. afflictio, fr. affligere.

affluence.etymology: F. affluence, L. affluentia, fr. affluens, p. pr. of affluere to flow to; ad + fluere to flow. See Flux.

affluent.etymology: Cf. F. affluent, L. affluens, -entis, p. pr. See Affluence.

afford.etymology: OE. aforthen, AS. gefor, for, to further, accomplish, afford, fr. for forth, forward. The prefix ge- has no well defined sense. See Forth.

roots.meaning: An Anglo-Saxon prefix. See Y-.

afforest.etymology: LL. afforestare; ad + forestare. See Forest.

affranchise.etymology: F. affranchir; (L. ad) + franc free. See Franchise and Frank.

affray.etymology: OE. afraien, affraien, OF. effreer, esfreer, F. effrayer, orig. to disquiet, put out of peace, fr. L. ex + OHG. fridu peace (akin to E. free). Cf. Afraid, Fray, Frith inclosure.

affricate.etymology: L. affricatus, p. p. of affricare to rub against; af- = ad- + fricare to rub.

roots.meaning: As a prefix ad- assumes the forms ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, assimilating the d with the first letter of the word to which ad- is prefixed. It remains unchanged before vowels, and before d, h, j, m, v. Examples: adduce, adhere, adjacent, admit, advent, accord, affect, aggregate, allude, annex, appear, etc. It becomes ac- before qu, as in acquiesce.

affright.etymology: Orig. p. p.; OE. afright, AS. afyrhtan to terrify; a- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + fyrhto fright. See Fright.

affront.etymology: OF. afronter, F. affronter, to confront, LL. affrontare to strike against, fr. L. ad + frons forehead, front. See Front.

afraid.etymology: OE. afrayed, affraide, p. p. of afraien to affray. See Affray, and cf. Afeard.

african.etymology: L. Africus, Africanus, fr. Afer African.

aft.etymology: AS. æftan behind; orig. superl. of of, off. See After.

after.etymology: AS. æfter after, behind; akin to Goth. aftaro, aftra, backwards, Icel. aptr, Sw. and Dan. efter, OHG. aftar behind, Dutch and LG. achter, Gr. -ter is an old comparative suffix, in E. generally -ther (as in other), and after is a compar. of of, off. Of; cf. Aft.

aftermost.etymology: OE. eftemest, AS. æftemest,akin to Gothic aftumist and aftuma, the last, orig. a superlative of of, with the superlative endings -te, -me, -st.

afterward.etymology: AS. æfteweard, a., behind. See Aft, and -ward (suffix). The final s in afterwards is adverbial, orig. a genitive ending.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

afterwards.etymology: AS. æfteweard, a., behind. See Aft, and -ward (suffix). The final s in afterwards is adverbial, orig. a genitive ending.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

aga.etymology: Turk. adha a great lord, chief master.

again.etymology: OE. agein, agayn, AS. ongegn, ongeán, against, again; on + geán, akin to Ger. gegewn against, Icel. gegn. Cf. Gainsay.

agama.etymology: From the Caribbean name of a species of lizard.

agaric.etymology: L. agaricum, Gr. Agara, a town in Sarmatia.

age.etymology: OF. aage, eage, F. âge, fr. L. aetas through a supposed LL. aetaticum. L. aetas is contracted fr. aevitas, fr. aevum lifetime, age; akin to E. aye ever. Cf. Each.

agency.etymology: agentia, fr. L. agens, agentis: cf. F. agence. See Agent.

agendum.etymology: L., neut. of the gerundive of agere to act.

agglomerate.etymology: L. agglomeratus, p. p. of agglomerare; ad + glomerare to form into a ball. See Glomerate.

agglutinate.etymology: L. agglutinatus, p. p. of agglutinare to glue or cement to a thing; ad + glutinare to glue; gluten glue. See Glue.

aggrandize.etymology: F. agrandir; à (L. ad) + grandir to increase, L. grandire, fr. grandis great. See Grand, and cf. Finish.

aggravate.etymology: L. aggravatus, p. p. of aggravare. See Aggrieve.

aggress.etymology: L. aggressus, p. p. of aggredi to go to, approach; ad + gradi to step, go, gradus step: cf. OF. aggresser. See Grade.

aggression.etymology: L. aggressio, fr. aggredi: cf. F. agression.

aggrieve.etymology: OE. agreven, OF. agrever; a (L. ad) + grever to burden, injure, L. gravare to weigh down, fr. gravis heavy. See Grieve, and cf. Aggravate.

aggroup.etymology: F. agrouper; à (L. ad) + groupe group. See Group..

agha.etymology: Turk. adha a great lord, chief master.

aghast.etymology: OE. agast, agasted, p. p. of agasten to terrify, fr. AS. pref. a- (cf. Goth. us-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + g to terrify, torment: cf. Goth. usgaisjan to terrify, primitively to fix, to root to the spot with terror; akin to L. haerere to stick fast, cling. See Gaze, Hesitate.

agile.etymology: F. agile, L. agilis, fr. agere to move. See Agent.

agility.etymology: F. agilié, L. agilitas, fr. agilis.

agio.etymology: It. aggio exchange, discount, premium, the same word as agio ease. See Ease.

agiotage.etymology: F. agiotage, fr. agioter to practice stockjobbing, fr. agio.

agitate.etymology: L. agitatus, p. p. of agitare to put in motion, fr. agere to move: cf. F. agiter. See Act, Agent.

aglet.etymology: F. aiguillette point, tagged point, dim. of aiguilee needle, fr. LL. acucula for acicula, dim. of L. acus needle, pinagleter to hook on. See Acute, and cf. Aiguillette.

agnail.etymology: AS. angnægl; ange vexation, trouble + nægel nail. Cf. Hangnail.

agnate.etymology: L. agnatus, p. p. of agnasci to be born in addition to; ad + nasci (for gnasci) to be born. Cf. Adnate.

agnize.etymology: Formed like recognize, fr. L. agnoscere.

ago.etymology: OE. ago, agon, p. p. of agon to go away, pass by, AS. agan to pass away; a- (cf. Goth. us-, Ger. er-, orig. meaning out) + gan to go. See Go.

agog.etymology: Cf. F. gogue fun, perhaps of Celtic origin.

agonize.etymology: F. agoniser, LL. agonizare, fr. Gr. Agony.

agony.etymology: L. agonia, Gr. agonie. See Agon.

agouti.etymology: F. agouti, acouti, Sp. aguti, fr. native name.

agriculture.etymology: L. agricultura; ager field + cultura cultivation: cf. F. agriculture. See Acre and Culture.

ague.etymology: OE. agu, ague, OF. agu, F. aigu, sharp, OF. fem. ague, LL. (febris) acuta, a sharp, acute fever, fr. L. acutus sharp. See Acute.

aid.etymology: F. aider, OF. aidier, fr. L. adjutare to help, freq. of adjuvare to help; ad + juvare to help. Cf. Adjutant.

aiglet.etymology: F. aiguillette point, tagged point, dim. of aiguilee needle, fr. LL. acucula for acicula, dim. of L. acus needle, pinagleter to hook on. See Acute, and cf. Aiguillette.

aigret.etymology: F., a sort of white heron, with a tuft of feathers on its head; a tuft of feathers; dim. of the same word as heron. See Heron, and cf. Egret, Egrette.

aigrette.etymology: F., a sort of white heron, with a tuft of feathers on its head; a tuft of feathers; dim. of the same word as heron. See Heron, and cf. Egret, Egrette.

aim.etymology: OE. amen, aimen, eimen, to guess at, to estimate, to aim, OF. esmer, asmer, fr. L. aestimare to estimate; or perh. fr. OF. aesmer; ad) + esmer. See Estimate.

air.etymology: OE. air, eir, F. air, L. aër, fr. Gr. wind. In sense 10 the French has taking a meaning fr. It. aria atmosphere, air, fr. the same Latin word; and in senses 11, 12, 13 the French meaning is either fr. L. aria, or due to confusion with F. aire, in an older sense of origin, descent. Cf. A, Debonair, Malaria, Wind.

aisle.etymology: OF. ele, F. aile, wing, wing of a building, L. ala, contr. fr. axilla.

aitchbone.etymology: For nachebone. For loss of n, cf. Adder. See Natch.

ajar.etymology: OE. on char ajar, on the turn; AS. cerr, cyrr, turn, akin to G. kehren to turn, and to D. akerre. See Char.

alabaster.etymology: L. alabaster, Gr. Alabastron, the name of a town in Egypt, near which it was common: cf. OF. alabastre, F. albâtre.

alacrity.etymology: L. alacritas, fr. alacer lively, eager, prob. akin to Gr. aljan zeal.

alanine.etymology: Aldehyde + the ending -ine. The -n- is a euphonic insertion.

roots.meaning: A suffix, indicating that those substances of whose names it is a part are basic, and alkaloidal in their nature.

alar.etymology: L. alarius, fr. ala wing: cf. F. alaire.

alarm.etymology: F. alarme, It. all' arme to arms ! fr. L. arma, pl., arms. See Arms, and cf. Alarum.

alarum.etymology: OE. alarom, the same word as alarm, n.

alas.etymology: OE. alas, allas, OF. alas, F. hélas; a interj. (L. ah.) + las wretched (that I am), L. lassus weary, akin to E. late. See Late.

alb.etymology: OE. albe, LL. alba, fr. L. albus white. Cf. Album and Aube.

albatross.etymology: Corrupt. fr. Pg. alcatraz cormorant, albatross, or Sp. alcatraz a pelican: cf. Pg. alcatruz, Sp. arcaduz, a bucket, fr. Ar. al-qadus the bucket, fr. Gr. ka`dos, a water vessel. So an Arabic term for pelican is water-carrier, as a bird carrying water in its pouch.

albescent.etymology: L. albescens, p. pr. of albescere to grow white, fr. albus white.

albigenses.etymology: From Albi and Albigeois, a town and its district in the south of France, in which the sect abounded.

albino.etymology: Sp. or Pg. albino, orig. whitish, fr. albo white, L. albus.

albion.etymology: Prob. from the same root as Gael. alp a height or hill. "It may have been bestowed on the land lying behind the white cliffs visible from the coast of Gaul. Albany, the old name of Scotland, means probably the "hilly land." I. Taylor.

album.etymology: L., neut. of albus white: cf. F. album. Cf. Alb.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

alcalde.etymology: Sp. alcalde, fr. Ar. al-qadi judge, fr. qada to decide, judge. Hence, the cadi of the Turks. Cf. Cadi.

alcazar.etymology: fr. Ar. al the + qacr (in pl.) a castle.

alchemy.etymology: OF. alkemie, arquemie, F. alchimie, Ar. al- kimia, fr. late Gr. alquimia, It. alchimia. Gr. fundere to pour, Goth. guitan, AS. geótan, to pour, and so to E. fuse. See Fuse, and cf. Chemistry.

roots.meaning: All; wholly; completely; as, almighty,almost. (b) Etym: [L. ad.]

alcohol.etymology: Cf. F. alcool, formerly written alcohol, Sp. alcohol alcohol, antimony, galena, OSp. alcofol; all fr. Ar. al-kohl a powder of antimony or galena, to paint the eyebrows with. The name was afterwards applied, on account of the fineness of this powder, to highly rectified spirits, a signification unknown in Arabia. The Sp. word has bot meanings. Cf. Alquifou.

alcove.etymology: F. alcôve, Sp. or Pg. alcoba, from Ar. al-quobbah arch, vault, tent.

aldebaran.etymology: Ar. al-debaran, fr. dabar to follow; so called because this star follows upon the Pleiades.

aldehyde.etymology: Abbrev. fr. alcohol dehydrogenatum, alcohol deprived of its hydrogen.

alder.etymology: OE. aldir, aller, fr. AS. alr, aler, alor, akin to D. els, G. erle, Icel. erlir, erli, Swed. al, Dan. elle, el, L. alnus, and E. elm.

alderman.etymology: AS. aldormon, ealdorman; ealdor an elder + man. See Elder, n.

ale.etymology: AS. ealu, akin to Icel., Sw., and Dan. öl, Lith. alus a kind of beer, OSlav. ol beer. Cf. Ir. ol drink, drinking.

aleatory.etymology: L. aleatorius, fr. alea chance, die.

alecost.etymology: Ale + L. costus an aromatic plant: cf. Costmary.

alembic.etymology: F. alambic (cf. Sp. alambique), Ar. al-anbiq, fr. Gr. alembic proper. Cf. Limbec.

alert.etymology: F. alerte, earlier à l'erte on the watch, fr. It. all' erta on the watch, prop. (standing) on a height, where one can look around; erta a declivity, steep, erto steep, p. p. of ergere, erigere, to erect, raise, L. erigere. See Erect.

aleutian.etymology: Said to be from the Russ. aleut a bold rock.

alewife.etymology: This word is properly aloof, the Indian name of a fish. See Winthrop on the culture of maize in America, "Phil Trans." No. 142, p. 1065, and Baddam's "Memoirs," vol. ii. p. 131.

alexanders.etymology: OE. alisaundre, OF. alissandere, fr. Alexander or Alexandria.

alfresco.etymology: It. al fresco in or on the fresh.

algebra.etymology: LL. algebra, fr. Ar. al-jebr reduction of parts to a whole, or fractions to whole numbers, fr. jabara to bind together, consolidate; al-jebr w'almuqabalah reduction and comparison (by equations): cf. F. algèbre, It. & Sp. algebra.

algid.etymology: L. algidus cold, fr. algere to be cold: cf. F. algide.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

algol.etymology: Ar. al-gh destruction, calamity, fr. ghala to take suddenly, destroy.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

alhambra.etymology: Ultimately fr. Ar. al the + hamra red; i. e., the red (sc. house).

alibi.etymology: L., elsewhere, at another place. See Alias.

alidade.etymology: LL. alidada, alhidada, fr. Ar. al-'idada a sort of rule: cf. F. alidade.

roots.meaning: All; wholly; completely; as, almighty,almost. (b) Etym: [L. ad.]

alien.etymology: OF. alien, L. alienus, fr. alius another; properly, therefore, belonging to another. See Else.

alienate.etymology: L. alienatus, p. p. of alienare, fr. alienus. See Alien, and cf. Aliene.

alienation.etymology: F. aliénation, L. alienatio, fr. alienare, fr. alienare. See Alienate.

alight.etymology: OE. alihten, fr. AS. alihtan; pref. a- (cf. Goth. us-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + lihtan, to alight, orig. to render light, to remove a burden from, fr. liht, leoht, light. See Light, v. i.

align.etymology: F. aligner; à (L. ad) + ligne (L. linea) line. See Line, and cf. Allineate.

alike.etymology: AS. onlic, gelic; pref. a + like.

aliment.etymology: L. alimentum, fr. alere to nourish; akin to Goth. alan to grow, Icel. ala to nourish: cf. F. aliment. See Old.

alimentary.etymology: L. alimentarius, fr. alimentum: cf. F. alimentaire.

alimony.etymology: L. alimonia, alimonium, nourishment, sustenance, fr. alere to nourish.

aliquant.etymology: L. aliquantus some, moderate; alius other + quantus how great: cf. F. aliquante.

aliquot.etymology: L. aliquot some, several; alius other + quot how many: cf. F. aliquote.

alive.etymology: OE. on live, AS. on life in life; life being dat. of lif life. See Life, and cf. Live, a.

alkahest.etymology: LL. alchahest, F. alcahest, a word that has an Arabic appearance, but was probably arbitrarily formed by Paracelsus.

alkali.etymology: F. alcali, ultimately fr. Ar. alqali ashes of the plant saltwort, fr. qalay to roast in a pan, fry.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

alkanet.etymology: Dim. of Sp. alcana, alhe, in which al is the Ar. article. See Henna, and cf. Orchanet.

all.etymology: OE. al, pl. alle, AS. eal, pl. ealle, Northumbrian alle, akin to D. & OHG. al, Ger. all, Icel. allr. Dan. al, Sw. all, Goth. alls; and perh. to Ir. and Gael. uile, W. oll.

allah.etymology: contr. fr. the article al the + ilah God.

allay.etymology: OE. alaien, aleggen, to lay down, put down, humble, put an end to, AS. alecgan; a- (cf. Goth. us-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + lecgan to lay; but confused with old forms of allege, alloy, alegge. See Lay.

allegation.etymology: L. allegatio, fr. allegare, allegatum, to send a message, cite; later, to free by giving reasons; ad + legare to send, commission. Cf. Allege and Adlegation.

allege.etymology: OE. aleggen to bring forward as evidence, OF. esligier to buy, prop. to free from legal difficulties, fr. an assumed LL. exlitigare; L. ex + litigare to quarrel, sue (see Litigate). The word was confused with L. allegare (see Allegation), and lex law. Cf. Allay.

allegiance.etymology: OE. alegeaunce; pref. a- + OF. lige, liege. The meaning was influenced by L. ligare to bind, and even by lex, legis, law. See Liege, Ligeance.

allegoric.etymology: F. allégorique, L. allegorius, fr. Gr. Allegory.

allegorical.etymology: F. allégorique, L. allegorius, fr. Gr. Allegory.

allegorize.etymology: Cf. F. allégoriser, fr. L. allegorizare.

allegro.etymology: It., merry, gay, fr. L. alacer lively. Cf. Aleger.

allelomorph.etymology: Gr. of one another + Gr. form.

alleviate.etymology: LL. alleviare, fr. L. ad + levis light. See Alegge, Levity.

alley.etymology: OE. aley, alley, OF. alée, F. allée, a going, passage, fr. OE. aler, F. aller, to go; of uncertain origin: cf. Prov. anar, It. andare, Sp. andar.

alliance.etymology: OE. aliaunce, OF. aliance, F. alliance, fr. OF. alier, F. allier. See Ally, and cf. LL. alligantia.

alligator.etymology: Sp. el lagarto the lizard (el lagarto de Indias, the cayman or American crocodile), fr. L. lacertus, lacerta, lizard. See Lizard.

alliteration.etymology: L. ad + litera letter. See Letter.

allocate.etymology: LL. allocatus, p. p. of allocare, fr. L. ad + locare to place. See Allow.

allocution.etymology: L. allocuto, fr. alloqui to speak to; ad + loqui to speak: cf. F. allocution.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

allopathy.etymology: Gr. allopathie, F. allopathie. See Pathos.

allot.etymology: OF. aloter, F. allotir; a (L. ad) + lot lot. See Lot.

allow.etymology: OE. alouen, OF. alouer, aloer, aluer, F. allouer, fr. LL. allocare to admit as proved, to place, use; confused with OF. aloer, fr. L. allaudare to extol; ad + laudare to praise. See Local, and cf. Allocate, Laud.

alloy.etymology: OE. alai, OF. alei, F. aloyer, to alloy, alier to ally. See Alloy, v. t.

allude.etymology: L. alludere to play with, to allude; ad + ludere to play.

allure.etymology: OF. aleurrer, alurer, fr. a (L. ad) + leurre lure. See Lure.

allusion.etymology: L. allusio, fr. alludere to allude: cf. F. allusion.

alluvion.etymology: F. alluvion, L. alluvio, fr. alluere to wash against; ad + luere, equiv. to lavare, to wash. See Lave.

alluvium.etymology: L., neut. of alluvius. See Alluvious.

ally.etymology: OE. alien, OF. alier, F. alier, fr. L. alligare to bind to; ad + ligare to bind. Cf. Alligate, Alloy, Allay, Ligament.

roots.meaning: A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.

almanac.etymology: LL. almanac, almanach: cf. F. almanach, Sp. almanaque, It. almanacco, all of uncertain origin.

almandine.etymology: LL. almandina, alamandina, for L. alabandina a precious stone, named after Alabanda, a town in Caria, where it was first and chiefly found: cf. F. almandine.

almighty.etymology: AS. ealmihtig, ælmihtig; eal (OE. al) ail + mihtig mighty.

almond.etymology: OE. almande, almaunde, alemaunde, F. amande, L. amygdala, fr. Gr. almendra. Cf. Amygdalate.

almoner.etymology: OE. aumener, aulmener, OF. almosnier, aumosnier, F. aumônier, fr. OF. almosne, alms, L. eleemosyna. See Alms.

almost.etymology: AS. ealmæst, ælmæst, quite the most, almost all; eal (OE. al) all + m most.

alms.etymology: OE. almes, almesse, AS. ælmysse, fr. L. eleemosyna, Gr. Almonry, Eleemosynary.

aloe.etymology: L. aloë, Gr. aloe, F. aloès.

aloft.etymology: Pref. a- + loft, which properly meant air. See Loft.

alone.etymology: All + one. OE. al one all allone, AS. an one, alone. See All, One, Lone.

along.etymology: OE. along, anlong, AS. andlang, along; pref. and- (akin to OFris. ond-, OHG. ant-, Ger. ent-, Goth. and-, anda-, L. ante, Gr. anti, over against) + lang long. See Long.

roots.meaning: See Anti-, prefix.
A prefix signifying within. See Ento-.

aloof.etymology: Pref. a- + loof, fr. D. loef luff, and so meaning, as a nautical word, to the windward. See Loof, Luff.

alp.etymology: L. Alpes the Alps, said to be of Celtic origin; cf. Gael. alp a high mountain, Ir. ailp any huge mass or lump: cf. F. Alpes.

alpaca.etymology: Sp. alpaca, fr. the original Peruvian name of the animal. Cf. Paco.

alpenstock.etymology: G.; Alp, gen. pl. Alpen + stock stick.

alpha.etymology: L. alpha, Gr. 'a`lfa, from Heb. aleph, name of the first letter in the alphabet, also meaning ox.

alphabet.etymology: L. alphabetum, fr. Gr. aleph and beth: cf. F. alphabet.

alpine.etymology: L. Alpinus, fr. Alpes the Alps: cf. F. Alpin.

also.etymology: All + so. OE. al so, AS. ealswa, alsw, ælswæ; eal, al, æl, all + swa so. See All, So, As.

altar.etymology: OE. alter, auter, autier, fr. L. altare, pl. altaria, altar, prob. fr. altus high: cf. OF. alter, autier, F. autel. Cf. Altitude.

alter.etymology: F. altérer, LL. alterare, fr. L. alter other, alius other. Cf. Else, Other.

altercate.etymology: L. altercatus, p. p. of altercare, altercari, fr. alter another. See Alter.

alternate.etymology: L. alternatus, p. p. of alternate, fr. alternus. See Altern, Alter.

altimeter.etymology: LL. altimeter; altus high + metrum, Gr. altimètre.

altitude.etymology: L. altitudo, fr. altus high. Cf. Altar, Haughty, Enhance.

alto.etymology: It. alto high, fr. L. altus. Cf. Alt.

altogether.etymology: OE. altogedere; al all + togedere together. See Together.

altruism.etymology: F. altruisme (a word of Comte's), It. altrui of or to others, fr. L. alter another.

altruistic.etymology: Cf. F. altruiste, a. See Altruism..

alula.etymology: NL., dim. of L. ala a wing.

alum.etymology: OE. alum, alom, OF. alum, F. alun, fr. L. alumen alum.

aluminiferous.etymology: L. alumen alum + -ferous: cf. F. aluminifère.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

aluminous.etymology: L. aluminosus, fr. alumen alum: cf. F. alumineux.

alveolar.etymology: L. alveolus a small hollow or cavity: cf. F. alvéolaire.

alveolus.etymology: L., a small hollow or cavity, dim. of alveus: cf. F. alvéole. See Alveary.

alvine.etymology: L. alvus belly: cf. F. alvin.

always.etymology: From Middle English alweyes , alwayes , alweys , a variant of Middle English alwey , alway ( “ always ” ) , from Old English ealneġ , ealne weġ ( “ always, perpetually ” , literally “ all the way, all the while, continuously ” ) , from ealne + weġ ( accusative case ) , equivalent to alway +‎ -s . Cognate with Scots always ( “ always ” ) , Low German allerwegens ( “ very often ” , literally “ all ways' ” ) . More at all , way .

amadavat.etymology: Indian name. From Ahmedabad, a city from which it was imported to Europe.

amain.etymology: Pref. a- + main. See 2d Main, n.

amanuensis.etymology: L., fr. a, ab + manus hand.

amass.etymology: F. ambusher, LL. amassare; L. ad + massa lump, mass. See Mass.

amateur.etymology: F., fr. L. amator lover, fr. amare to love.

amative.etymology: L. amatus, p. p. of amare to love.

ambages.etymology: L. (usually in pl.); pref. ambi-, amb- + agere to drive: cf. F. ambage.

roots.meaning: A prefix meaning about, around; -- used in words derived from the Latin.
A prefix meaning about, around; -- used in words derived from the Latin.

amber.etymology: OE. aumbre, F. ambre, Sp. ámbar, and with the Ar. article, alámbar, fr. Ar. 'anbar ambergris.

ambergris.etymology: F. ambre gris, i. e., gray amber; F. gris gray, which is of German origin: cf. OS. grîs, G. greis, gray-haired. See Amber.

ambient.etymology: L. ambiens, p. pr. of ambire to go around; amb- + ire to go.

roots.meaning: A prefix meaning about, around; -- used in words derived from the Latin.

ambiguity.etymology: L. ambiguitas, fr. ambiguus: cf. F. ambiguité.

ambiguous.etymology: L. ambiguus, fr. ambigere to wander about, waver; amb- + agere to drive.

roots.meaning: A prefix meaning about, around; -- used in words derived from the Latin.

ambit.etymology: L. ambitus circuit, fr. ambire to go around. See Ambient.

ambition.etymology: F. ambition, L. ambitio a going around, especially of candidates for office is Rome, to solicit votes (hence, desire for office or honorambire to go around. See Ambient, Issue.

ambitious.etymology: L. ambitiosus: cf. F. ambitieux. See Ambition.

amble.etymology: F. ambler to amble, fr. L. ambulare to walk, in LL., to amble, perh. fr. amb-, ambi-, and a root meaning to go: cf. Gr. base. Cf. Ambulate.

ambrosia.etymology: L. ambrosia, Gr. mrita, L. mortuus, dead, and to E. mortal.

ambulacrum.etymology: L., an alley or covered way.

ambulance.etymology: F. ambulance, hôpital ambulant, fr. L. ambulare to walk. See Amble.

ambulant.etymology: L. ambulans, p. pr. of ambulare to walk: cf. F. ambulant.

ambulate.etymology: L. ambulare to walk. See Amble.

ambuscade.etymology: F. embuscade, fr. It. imboscata, or Sp. emboscada, fr. emboscar to ambush, fr. LL. imboscare. See Ambush, v. t.

ambush.etymology: F. embûche, fr. the verb. See Ambush, v. t.

ameliorate.etymology: L. ad + meliorare to make better: cf. F. améliorer. See Meliorate.

amen.etymology: L. amen, Gr. am certainly, truly.

amenable.etymology: F. amener to lead; ad) = mener to lead, fr. L. minare to drive animals (properly by threatening cries), in LL. to lead; L. minari, to threaten, minae threats. See Menace.

amend.etymology: F. amender, L. emendare; e(ex) + mendum, menda, fault, akin to Skr. minda personal defect. Cf. Emend, Mend.

amends.etymology: F. amendes, pl. of amende. Cf. Amende.

amenity.etymology: F. aménité, L. amoenitas, fr. amoenus pleasant.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

amerce.etymology: OF. amercier, fr. a merci at the mercy of, liable to a punishment. See Mercy.

amethyst.etymology: F. ametiste, amatiste, F. améthyste, L. amethystus, fr. Gr. Mead.

amiable.etymology: F. amiable, L. amicabilis friendly, fr. amicus friend, fr. amare to love. The meaning has been influenced by F. aimable, L. amabilis lovable, fr. amare to love. Cf. Amicable, Amorous, Amability.

amicable.etymology: L. amicabilis, fr. amicus friend, fr. amare to love. See Amiable.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to denote: (a) The nonmetallic, or negative, element or radical in a binary compound; as, oxide, sulphide, chloride. (b) A compound which is an anhydride; as, glycolide, phthalide. (c) Any one of a series of derivatives; as, indogenide, glucoside, etc.
A suffix, indicating that those substances of whose names it is a part are basic, and alkaloidal in their nature.

amity.etymology: F. amitié, OF. amistié, amisté, fr. an assumed LL. amisitas, fr. L. amicus friendly, from amare to love. See Amiable.

ammonia.etymology: From sal ammoniac, which was first obtaining near the temple of Jupiter Ammon, by burning camel's dung. See Ammoniac.

ammoniac.etymology: L. Ammoniacum, Gr. Ammon; cf. F. ammoniac. See Ammonite.

ammonite.etymology: L. cornu Ammonis born of Ammon; L. Ammon, Gr. Amun.

ammunition.etymology: F. amunition, for munition, prob. caused by taking la munition as l'amunition. See Munition.

amnesty.etymology: L. amnestia, Gr. amnistie, earlier amnestie. See Mean, v.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

amorous.etymology: OF. amoros, F. amoreux, LL. amorosus, fr. L. amor love, fr. amare to love.

amort.etymology: Pref. a- + F. mort death, dead; all amort is for alamort.

amortization.etymology: LL. amortisatio, admortizatio. See Amortize, and cf. Admortization.

amortize.etymology: OE. amortisen, LL. amortisare, admortizare, F. amortir to sell in mortmain, to extinguish; L. ad + mors death. See Mortmain

amount.etymology: OF. amonter to increase, advance, ascend, fr. amont (equiv. to L. ad montem to the mountain) upward, F. amont up the river. See Mount, n.

ampere.etymology: From the name of a French electrician.

ampersand.etymology: A corruption of and, per se and, i. e., & by itself makes and.

amphibole.etymology: Gr. amphibole. Haüy so named the genus from the great variety of color and composition assumed by the mineral.

amphibology.etymology: L. amphibologia, for amphibolia, fr. Gr. logia as if fr. Gr. amphibologie. See Amphiboly.

amphiboly.etymology: L. amphibolia, Gr. amphibolie. See Amphibolous.

amphiprostyle.etymology: L. amphiprostylos, Gr. amphiprostyle. See Prostyle.

amphitheater.etymology: L. amphitheatrum, fr. Gr. amphithé\'83tre. See Theater.

amphitheatre.etymology: L. amphitheatrum, fr. Gr. amphithé\'83tre. See Theater.

ample.etymology: F. ample, L. amplus, prob. for ambiplus full on both sides, the last syllable akin to L. plenus full. See Full, and cf. Double.

amplify.etymology: F. amplifier, L. amplificare. See Ample, -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

amplitude.etymology: L. amplitudo, fr. amplus: cf. F. amplitude. See Ample.

ampul.etymology: AS. ampella, ampolla, L. ampulla: cf. OF. ampolle, F. ampoule.

amputate.etymology: L. amputatus, p. p. of amputare: amb- + putare to prune, putus clean, akin to E. pure. See Putative.

amuse.etymology: F. amuser to make stay, to detain, to amuse, ad) + OF. muser. See Muse, v.

amygdala.etymology: L., an almond, fr. Gr. 'amygda`lh. See Almond.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.

A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

ana.etymology: The neut. pl. ending of Latin adjectives in -anus.

anabaptism.etymology: L. anabaptismus, Gr. anabaptisme. See Anabaptize.

anabaptist.etymology: LL. anabaptista, fr. Gr. as if : cf. F. anabaptiste.

anaesthesia.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. anesthésie. See Æsthetics.

anagram.etymology: F. anagramme, LL. anagramma, fr. Gr. Graphic.

analogy.etymology: L. analogia, Gr. analogie. See Analogous.

ananas.etymology: Sp. ananas, from the native American name.

anastomose.etymology: Cf. F. anastomoser, fr. anastomose. See Anastomosis.

anathema.etymology: L. anath, fr. Gr. anath, fr. Gr. Thesis.

anatomic.etymology: L. anatomicus, Gr. anatomique. See Anatomy.

anatomical.etymology: L. anatomicus, Gr. anatomique. See Anatomy.

ancestor.etymology: OE. ancestre, auncestre, also ancessour; the first forms fr. OF. ancestre, F. ancêtre, fr. the L. nom. antessor one who goes before; the last form fr. OF. ancessor, fr. L. acc. antecessorem, fr. antecedere to go before; ante before + cedere to go. See Cede, and cf. Antecessor.

anchor.etymology: OE. anker, AS. ancor, oncer, L. ancora, sometimes spelt anchora, fr. Gr. angle: cf. F. ancre. See Angle, n.

anchorite.etymology: F. anachorète, L. anachoreta, fr. Gr. ha to leave. Cf. Anchor a hermit.

anchovy.etymology: Sp. anchoa, anchova, or Pg. anchova, prob. of Iberian origin, and lit. a dried or pickled fish, fr. Bisc. antzua dry: cf. D. anchovis, F. anchois.

ancient.etymology: OE. auncien, F. ancien, LL. antianus, fr. L. ante before. See Ante-, pref.

roots.meaning: A Latin preposition and prefix; akin to Gr. anti, Goth. and-, anda- (only in comp.), AS. and-, ond-, (only in comp.: cf. Answer, Along), G. ant-, ent- (in comp.). The Latin ante is generally used in the sense of before, in regard to position, order, or time, and the Gr. opposite, or in the place of.

ancillary.etymology: L. ancillaris, fr. ancilla a female servant.

andante.etymology: It. andante, p. pr. of andare to go.

andiron.etymology: OE. anderne, aunderne, aundyre, OF. andier, F. landier, fr. LL. andena, andela, anderia, of unknown origin. The Eng. was prob. confused with brand-iron, AS. brand-isen.

anecdote.etymology: F. anecdote, fr. Gr. Dose, n.

anele.etymology: OE. anelien; an on + AS. ele oil, L. oleum. See Oil, Anoil.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.
A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

anfractuous.etymology: L. anfractuosus, fr. anfractus a turning, a winding, fr. the unused anfringere to wind, bend; an-, for amb- + fractus, p. p. of frangere to break: cf. F. anfractueux.

roots.meaning: A prefix meaning about, around; -- used in words derived from the Latin.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

angina.etymology: L., fr. angere to strangle, to choke. See Anger, n.

roots.meaning: A prefix, or combining form, in numerous compounds, usually relating to seed or blood vessels, or to something contained in, or covered by, a vessel.
A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.
A prefix, or combining form, in numerous compounds, usually relating to seed or blood vessels, or to something contained in, or covered by, a vessel.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.
