A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

angle.etymology: F. angle, L. angulus angle, corner; akin to uncus hook, Gr. angel hook, fish-hook, G. angel, and F. anchor.

anglican.etymology: Angli the Angles, a Germanic tribe in Lower Germany. Cf. English.

anguish.etymology: OE. anguishe, anguise, angoise, F. angoisse, fr. L. angustia narrowness, difficulty, distress, fr. angustus narrow, difficult, fr. angere to press together. See Anger.

angular.etymology: L. angularis, fr. angulus angle, corner. See Angle.

angulate.etymology: L. angulatus, p. p. of angulare to make angular.

anil.etymology: F. anil, Sp. anil, or Pg. anil; all fr. Ar. an-nil, for al-nil the indigo plant, fr. Skr. nila dark blue, nili indigo, indigo plant. Cf. Lilac.

anile.etymology: L. anilis, fr. anus an old woman.

animadversion.etymology: L. animadversio, fr. animadvertere: cf. F. animadversion. See Animadvert.

animadvert.etymology: L. animadvertere; animus mind + advertere to turn to; ad to + vertere to turn.

animal.etymology: L., fr. anima breath, soul: cf. F. animal. See Animate.

animalcule.etymology: As if fr. a L. animalculum, dim. of animal.

animate.etymology: L. animatus, p. p. of animare, fr. anima breath, soul; akin to animus soul, mind, Gr. an to breathe, live, Goth. us-anan to expire (us- out), Icel. önd breath, anda to breathe, OHG. ando anger. Cf. Animal.

animism.etymology: Cf. F. animisme, fr. L. anima soul. See Animate.

animosity.etymology: F. animosité, fr. L. animositas. See Animose, Animate, v. t.

ankle.etymology: OE. ancle, anclow, AS. ancleow; akin to Icel. ökkla, ökli, Dan. and Sw. ankel, D. enklaauw, enkel, G. enkel, and perh. OHG. encha, ancha thigh, shin: cf. Skr. anga limb, anguri finger. Cf. Haunch.

annals.etymology: L. annalis (sc. liber), and more frequently in the pl. annales (sc. libri), chronicles, fr. annus year. Cf. Annual.

anneal.etymology: OE. anelen to heat, burn, AS. an; an on + to burn; also OE. anelen to enamel, prob. influenced by OF. neeler, nieler, to put a black enamel on gold or silver, F. nieller, fr. LL. nigellare to blacken, fr. L. nigellus blackish, dim. of niger black. Cf. Niello, Negro.

annelid.etymology: F. annélide, fr. anneler to arrange in rings, OF. anel a ring, fr. L. anellus a ring, dim. of annulus a ring.

annelidan.etymology: F. annélide, fr. anneler to arrange in rings, OF. anel a ring, fr. L. anellus a ring, dim. of annulus a ring.

annex.etymology: F. annexer, fr. L. annexus, p. p. of annectere to tie or bind to; ad + nectere to tie, to fasten together, akin to Skr. nah to bind.

annexation.etymology: Cf. F. annexation. See Annex, v. t.

annihilate.etymology: L. annihilare; ad + nihilum, nihil, nothing, ne hilum (filum) not a thread, nothing at all. Cf. File, a row.

anniversary.etymology: L. anniversarius; annus year + vertere, versum, to turn: cf. F. anniversaire.

annotate.etymology: L. annotatus; p. p. of annotare to annotate; ad + notare to mark, nota mark. See Note, n.

announce.etymology: OF. anoncier, F. annoncer, fr. L. annuntiare; ad + nuntiare to report, relate, nuntius messenger, bearer of news. See Nuncio, and cf. Annunciate.

annoy.etymology: OE. anoien, anuien, OF. anoier, anuier, F. ennuyer, fr. OF. anoi, anui, enui, annoyance, vexation, F. ennui. See Annoy, n.

annual.etymology: OE. annuel, F. annuel, fr. L. annualis, fr. annus year. Cf. Annals.

annuity.etymology: LL. annuitas, fr. L. annus year: cf. F. annuité.

annul.etymology: F. annuler, LL. annullare, annulare, fr. L. ad to + nullus none, nullum, neut., nothing. See Null, a.

annular.etymology: L. annularis, fr. annulis ring: cf. F. annulaire.

anoint.etymology: OF. enoint, p. p. of enoindre, fr. L. inungere; in + ungere, unguere, to smear, anoint. See Ointment, Unguent.

anolis.etymology: In the Antilles, anoli, anoalli, a lizard.

anomalous.etymology: L. anomalus, Gr. Same, and cf. Abnormal.

anon.etymology: OE. anoon, anon, anan, lit., in one (moment), fr. AS. on in + an one. See On and One.

anserine.etymology: L. anserinus, fr. anser a goose.

answer.etymology: From Middle English answere , andsware , from Old English andswaru ( “ answer ” ) , from and- ( “ against ” ) +‎ swaru ( “ affirmation ” ) , (from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- ( “ front, forehead ” ) and Old English swerian ( “ to swear ” ) , from Proto-Indo-European *swer- ), suggesting an original meaning of "a sworn statement rebutting a charge". The cognates suggest the existence of Proto-Germanic *andaswarō ( “ a reply to a question ” ) . Cognate with Old Frisian ondser ( “ answer ” ) , Old Saxon andswōr ( “ answer ” ) , Danish and Swedish ansvar ( “ liability, responsibility, answer ” ) , Icelandic andsvar ( “ answer, response ” ) . Compare also Old English andwyrde ( “ answer ” ) (cognate to Dutch antwoord , German Antwort ), Old English andcwiss ( “ reply ” ) , German Schwur ( “ oath, vow ” ) .

ant.etymology: OE. ante, amete, emete, AS. æmete akin to G. ameise. Cf. Emmet.

antagonist.etymology: L. antagonista, Gr. antagoniste. See Antagonism.

antarctic.etymology: OE. antartik, OF. antartique, F. antarctique, L. antarcticus, fr. Gr. Arctic.

antecede.etymology: L. antecedere; ante + cedere to go. See Cede.

antecedent.etymology: L. antecedens, -entis, p. pr. of antecedere: cf. F. antécédent.

roots.meaning: A Latin preposition and prefix; akin to Gr. anti, Goth. and-, anda- (only in comp.), AS. and-, ond-, (only in comp.: cf. Answer, Along), G. ant-, ent- (in comp.). The Latin ante is generally used in the sense of before, in regard to position, order, or time, and the Gr. opposite, or in the place of.

antemeridian.etymology: L. antemeridianus; ante + meridianus belonging to midday or noon. See Meridian.

antenna.etymology: L. antenna sail-yard; NL., a feeler, horn of an insect.

antepenult.etymology: L. antepaenultima (sc. syllaba) antepenultimate; ante before + paenultimus the last but one; paene almost + ultimus last.

antepenultima.etymology: L. antepaenultima (sc. syllaba) antepenultimate; ante before + paenultimus the last but one; paene almost + ultimus last.

anterior.etymology: L. anterior, comp. of ante before.

anthem.etymology: OE. antym, antefne, AS. antefen, fr. LL. antiphona, fr. Gr. anthaine, anteine, antieune, F. antienne. See Antiphon.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

anthracite.etymology: L. anthracites a kind of bloodstone; fr. Gr. Anthrax.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

antic.etymology: The same word as antique; cf. It. antico ancient. See Antique.

anticipant.etymology: L. anticipans, p. pr. of anticipare.

anticipate.etymology: L. anticipatus, p. p. of anticipare to anticipate; ante + capere to make. See Capable.

antidote.etymology: L. antidotum, Gr. antidote. See Dose, n.

antipathy.etymology: L. antipathia, Gr. antipathie. See Pathos.

antiquary.etymology: L. antiquarius, fr. antiquus ancient. See Antique.

antiquate.etymology: L. antiquatus, p. p. of antiquare, fr. antiquus ancient.

antique.etymology: F., fr. L. antiquus old, ancient, equiv. to anticus, from ante before. Cf. Antic.

antiquity.etymology: L. antiquitas, fr. antiquus: cf. F. antiquité. See Antique.

antler.etymology: OE. auntelere, OF. antoillier, andoiller, endouiller, fr. F. andouiller, fr. an assumed LL. antocularis, fr. L. ante before + oculus eye. See Ocular.

antrorse.etymology: From L. ante + versun turned; apparently formed in imitation of re.

anus.etymology: L., prob. for asnus: cf. Gr. as.

anvil.etymology: OE. anvelt, anfelt, anefelt, AS. anfilt, onfilt; of uncertain origin; cf. OHG. anafalz, D. aanbeld.

anxiety.etymology: L. anxietas, fr. anxius: cf. F. anxiété. See Anxious.

anxious.etymology: L. anxius, fr. angere to cause pain, choke; akin to Gr. Anger.

any.etymology: OE. æni, æni, eni, ani, oni, AS. ænig, fr. an one. It is akin to OS. enig, OHG. einic, G. einig, D. eenig. See One.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

apace.etymology: Pref. a- + pace. OE. a pas at a walk, in which a is the article. See Pace.

apart.etymology: F. à part; (L. ad) + part part. See Part.

apartment.etymology: F. appartement; cf. It. appartamento, fr. appartare to separate, set apart; all fr. L. ad + pars, partis, part. See Apart.

apathy.etymology: L. apathia, Gr. apathie. See Pathos.

ape.etymology: AS. apa; akin to D. aap, OHG. affo, G. affe, Icel. api, Sw. apa, Dan. abe, W. epa.

apercu.etymology: F., prop. p. p. of apercevoir to perceive.

aperient.etymology: L. aperiens, p. pr. of aperire to uncover, open; ab + parire, parere, to bring forth, produce. Cf. Cover, Overt.

aperture.etymology: L. apertura, fr. aperire. See Aperient.

apical.etymology: L. apex, apicis, tip or summit.

aplomb.etymology: F., lit. perpendicularity; plomb lead. See Plumb.

apology.etymology: L. apologia, Gr. apologie. See Apologetic.

apoplectic.etymology: L. apoplecticus, Gr. apoplectique. See Apoplexy.

apoplexy.etymology: OE. poplexye, LL. poplexia, apoplexia, fr. Gr. apoplexie. See Plague.

apostasy.etymology: OE. apostasie, F. apostasie, L. apostasia, fr. Gr. Off and Stand.

apostle.etymology: OE. apostle, apostel, postle, AS. apostol, L. apostolus, fr. Gr. stellen to set, E. stall: cf. F. apôtre, Of. apostre, apostle, apostele, apostole.

apostrophize.etymology: imp. & p. p. Apostrophized; p. pr. & vb. n. Apostrophizing.

apothecary.etymology: OE. apotecarie, fr. LL. apothecarius, fr. L. apotheca storehouse, Gr. apo, fr. apothicaire, OF. apotecaire. See Thesis.

appall.etymology: OF. appalir to grow pale, make pale; a (L. ad) + pâlir to grow pale, to make pale, pâle pale. See Pale, a., and cf. Pall.

appanage.etymology: F. apanage, fr. OF. apaner to nourish, support, fr. LL. apanare to furnish with bread, to provision; L. ad + pains bread.

apparatus.etymology: L., from apparare, apparatum, to prepare; ad + prepare to make ready.

apparel.etymology: OE. apparel, apareil, OF. apareil, appareil, preparation, provision, furniture, OF. apareiller to match, prepare, F. appareiller; OF. a (L. ad) + pareil like, similar, fr. LL. pariculus, dim. of L. par equal. See Pair.

apparent.etymology: F. apparent, L. apparens, -entis, p. pr. of apparere. See Appear.

apparition.etymology: F. apparition, L. apparitio, fr. apparere. See Appear.

appeal.etymology: OE. appelen, apelen, to appeal, accuse, OF. appeler, fr. L. appellare to approach, address, invoke, summon, call, name; akin to appellere to drive to; ad + pellere to drive. See Pulse, and cf. Peal.

appear.etymology: OE. apperen, aperen, OF. aparoir, F. apparoir, fr. L. appar to appear + parto come forth, to be visible; prob. from the same root as par to produce. Cf. Apparent, Parent, Peer, v. i.

appearance.etymology: F. apparence, L. apparentia, fr. apparere. See Appear.

appease.etymology: OE. apesen, apaisen, OF. apaisier, apaissier, F. apaiser, fr. a (L. ad) + OF. pais peace, F. paix, fr. L. pax, pacis. See Peace.

appellant.etymology: L. appellans, p. pr. of appellare; cf. F. appelant. See Appeal.

appellate.etymology: L. appelatus, p. p. of appellare.

appellation.etymology: L. appellatio, fr. appellare: cf. F. appellation. See Appeal.

appellative.etymology: L. appellativus, fr. appellare: cf. F. appelatif. See Appeal.

append.etymology: L. appendere or F. appendre: cf. OE. appenden, apenden, to belong, OF. apendre, F. appendre, fr. L. append, v. i., to hang to, append, v. t., to hang to; ad + pend, v. i., to hang, pend, v. t., to hang. See Pendant.

appendant.etymology: F. appendant, p. pr. of appendre. See Append, v. t.

appendix.etymology: L. appendix, -dicis, fr. appendere. See Append.

apperceive.etymology: F. apercevoir, fr. L. ad + percipere, perceptum, to perceive. See Perceive.

apperception.etymology: Pref. ad- + perception: cf. F. apperception.

roots.meaning: As a prefix ad- assumes the forms ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, assimilating the d with the first letter of the word to which ad- is prefixed. It remains unchanged before vowels, and before d, h, j, m, v. Examples: adduce, adhere, adjacent, admit, advent, accord, affect, aggregate, allude, annex, appear, etc. It becomes ac- before qu, as in acquiesce.

appertain.etymology: OE. apperteinen, apertenen, OF. apartenir, F. appartenir, fr. L. appertinere; ad + pertinere to reach to, belong. See Pertain.

appetency.etymology: L. appetentia, fr. appetere to strive after, long for. See Appetite.

appetent.etymology: L. appetens, p. pr. of appetere.

appetite.etymology: OE. appetit, F. appétit, fr. L. appetitus, fr. appetere to strive after, long for; ad + petere to seek. See Petition, and cf. Appetence.

applaud.etymology: L. applaudere; ad + plaudere to clash, to clap the hands: cf. F. applaudir. Cf. Explode.

apple.etymology: OE. appel, eppel, AS. æppel, æpl; akin to Fries. & D. appel, OHG, aphul, aphol, G. apfel, Icel. epli, Sw. äple, Dan. æble, Gael. ubhall, W. afal, Arm. aval, Lith. ob, Russ. iabloko; of unknown origin.

applicable.etymology: Cf. F. aplicable, fr. L. applicare. See Apply.

applicant.etymology: L. applicans, p. pr. of applicare. See Apply.

application.etymology: L. applicatio, fr. applicare: cf. F. application. See Apply.

applicative.etymology: Cf. F. applicatif, fr. L. applicare. See Apply.

applique.etymology: F., fr. appliquer to put on.

apply.etymology: OF. aplier, F. appliquer, fr. L. applicare to join, fix, or attach to; ad + plicare to fold, to twist together. See Applicant, Ply.

appoggiatura.etymology: It., fr. appogiarre to lean, to rest; ap- (L. ad) + poggiare to mount, ascend, poggio hill, fr. L. podium an elevated place.

appoint.etymology: OE. appointen, apointen, OF. apointier to prepare, arrange, lean, place, F. appointer to give a salary, refer a cause, fr. LL. appunctare to bring back to the point, restore, to fix the point in a controversy, or the points in an agreement; L. ad + punctum a point. See Point.

appointee.etymology: F. appointé, p. p. of appointer. See Appoint, v. t.

apportion.etymology: OF. apportionner, LL. apportionare, fr. L. ad + portio. See Portion.

appose.etymology: F. apposer to set to; ad) + poser to put, place. See Pose.

apposite.etymology: L. appositus, p. p. of apponere to set or put to; ad + ponere to put, place.

apposition.etymology: L. appositio, fr. apponere: cf. F. apposition. See Apposite.

appraise.etymology: Pref. ad- + praise. See Praise, Price, Apprize, Appreciate.

roots.meaning: As a prefix ad- assumes the forms ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, assimilating the d with the first letter of the word to which ad- is prefixed. It remains unchanged before vowels, and before d, h, j, m, v. Examples: adduce, adhere, adjacent, admit, advent, accord, affect, aggregate, allude, annex, appear, etc. It becomes ac- before qu, as in acquiesce.

appreciate.etymology: L. appretiatus, p. p. of appretiare to value at a price, appraise; ad + pretiare to prize, pretium price. Cf. Appraise.

apprehend.etymology: L. apprehendere; ad + prehendere to lay hold of, seize; prae before + -hendere (used only in comp.); akin to Gr. get: cf. F. appréhender. See Prehensile, Get.

apprehension.etymology: L. apprehensio: cf. F. appréhension. See Apprehend.

apprentice.etymology: OE. apprentice, prentice, OF. aprentis, nom. of aprentif, fr. apprendare to learn, L. apprendere, equiv. to apprehendere, to take hold of (by the mind), to comprehend. See Apprehend, Prentice.

appressed.etymology: p. p. appress, which is not in use. See Adpress.

apprise.etymology: F. appris, fem. apprise, p. p. apprendre to learn, to teach, to inform. Cf. Apprehend, Apprentice.

apprize.etymology: The same as Appraise, only more accommodated to the English form of the L. pretiare.

approach.etymology: OE. approchen, aprochen, OF. approcher, LL. appropriare, fr. L. ad + propiare to draw near, prope near.

approbate.etymology: L. approbatus, p. p. of approbare to approve.

approbation.etymology: L. approbatio: cf. F. approbation. See Approve to prove.

appropriate.etymology: L. appropriatus, p. p. of appropriare; ad + propriare to appropriate, fr. proprius one's own, proper. See Proper.

approve.etymology: OE. aproven, appreven, to prove, OF. aprover, F. approuver, to approve, fr. L. approbare; ad + probare to esteem as good, approve, prove. See Prove, and cf. Approbate.

approximate.etymology: L. approximatus, p. p. of approximare to approach; ad + proximare to come near. See Proximate.

appurtenance.etymology: OF. apurtenaunce, apartenance, F. appartenance, LL. appartenentia, from L. appertinere. See Appertain.

appurtenant.etymology: F. appartenant, p. pr. of appartenir. See Appurtenance.

apricot.etymology: OE. apricock, abricot, F. abricot, fr. Sp. albaricoque or Pg. albricoque, fr. Ar. albirq, al-burq. Though the E. and F. form abricot is derived from the Arabic through the Spanish, yet the Arabic word itself was formed from the Gr. praecoquus, praecox, early ripe. The older E. form apricock was prob. taken direct from Pg. See Precocious, Cook.

april.etymology: L. Aprilis. OE. also Averil, F. Avril, fr. L. Aprilis.

apron.etymology: OE. napron, OF. naperon, F. napperon, dim. of OF. nape, F. nappe, cloth, tablecloth, LL. napa, fr. L. mappa, napkin, table napkin. See Map.

apropos.etymology: F. ad) + propos purpose, L. proposium plan, purpose, fr. proponere to propose. See Propound.

apt.etymology: F. apte, L. aptus, fr. obsolete apere to fasten, to join, to fit, akin to apisci to reach, attain: cf. Gr. apta fit, fr. ap to reach attain.

aptitude.etymology: F. aptitude, LL. aptitudo, fr. L. aptus. See Apt, and cf. Attitude.

aquarius.etymology: L. aquarius, adj., relating to water, and n., a water-carrier, fr. aqua. See Aqua.

aquatic.etymology: L. aquaticus: cf. F. aquatique. See Aqua.

aquatint.etymology: It. acquatinta dyed water; acqua (L. aqua) water + tinto, fem. tinta, dyed. See Tint.

aqueduct.etymology: F. aqueduc, OF. aqueduct (Cotgr.), fr. L. aquaeductus; aquae, gen. of aqua water + ductus a leading, ducere to lead. See Aqua, Duke.

aqueous.etymology: Cf. F. aqueux, L. aquosus, fr. aqua. See Aqua, Aquose.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

aquiline.etymology: L. aquilinus, fr. aquila eagle: cf. F. aquilin. See Eagle.

arabesque.etymology: F. arabesque, fr. It. arabesco, fr. Arabo Arab.

arable.etymology: F. arable, L. arabilis, fr. arare to plow, akin to Gr. ear, to plow. See Earable.

aramaean.etymology: L. Aramaeus, Gr. Aram, i. e. Highland, a name given to Syria and Mesopotamia.

aramean.etymology: L. Aramaeus, Gr. Aram, i. e. Highland, a name given to Syria and Mesopotamia.

araucaria.etymology: Araucania, a territory south of Chili.

arbalest.etymology: OF. arbaleste, LL. arbalista, for L. arcuballista; arcus bow + ballista a military engine. See Ballista.

arbalist.etymology: OF. arbaleste, LL. arbalista, for L. arcuballista; arcus bow + ballista a military engine. See Ballista.

arbiter.etymology: L. arbiter; ar- (for ad) + the root of betere to go; hence properly, one who comes up to look on.

arbitrable.etymology: Cf. F. arbitrable, fr. L. arbitrari. See Arbitrate, v. t.

arbitrage.etymology: F., fr. arbiter to give judgment, L. arbitrari.

arbitrary.etymology: L. arbitrarius, fr. arbiter: cf. F. arbitraire. See Arbiter.

arbitrate.etymology: L. arbitratus, p. p. of arbitrari to be a hearer or beholder of something, to make a decision, to give judgment, fr. arbiter. See Arbiter.

arbitration.etymology: F. arbitration, L. arbitratio, fr. arbitrari.

arbitrator.etymology: L., fr. arbitrari: cf. F. arbitrateur.

arbor.etymology: OE. herber, herbere, properly a garden of herbs, F. herbier, fr. L. herbarium. See Herb, and cf. Herbarium.

arborescent.etymology: L. arborescens, p. pr. of arborescere to become a tree, fr. arbor tree.

arboretum.etymology: L., a place grown with trees.

arboriculture.etymology: L. arbor tree + cultura. See Culture.

arborist.etymology: F. arboriste, fr. L. arbor tree.

arbutus.etymology: L. arbutus, akin to arbor tree.

arc.etymology: F. arc, L. arcus bow, arc. See Arch, n.

arcade.etymology: F. arcade, Sp. arcada, LL. arcata, fr. L. arcus bow, arch.

arcadian.etymology: L. Arcadius, Arcadicus, fr. Arcadia: cf. F. Arcadien, Arcadique.

arcadic.etymology: L. Arcadius, Arcadicus, fr. Arcadia: cf. F. Arcadien, Arcadique.

arcanum.etymology: L., fr. arcanus closed, secret, fr. arca chest, box, fr. arcere to inclose. See Ark.

arch.etymology: F. arche, fr. LL. arca, for arcus. See Arc.

archangel.etymology: L. archangelus, Gr. archangel, F. archange. See Arch-, pref., and Angel.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying chief, as in archbuilder, archfiend.

archbishop.etymology: AS. arcebisceop, arcebiscop, L. archiepiscopus, fr. Gr. Bishop.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying dominion, jurisdiction; as, bishopric, the district over which a bishop exercises authority.

archdeacon.etymology: AS. arcediacon, archidiacon, L. archidiaconus, fr. Gr. Arch-, pref., and Deacon.

archer.etymology: archier, F. archer, LL. arcarius, fr. L. arcus bow. See Arc, Arch, n.

archetype.etymology: L. archetypum, Gr. archétype. See Arch-, pref.

archil.etymology: OF. orchel, orcheil, It. orcella, oricello, or OSp. orchillo. Cf. Orchil.

archipelago.etymology: It. arcipelago, properly, chief sea; Gr. pref Plague.

architect.etymology: L. architectus, architecton, Gr. archi-) + architecte, It. architetto. See Technical.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying chief, arch; as, architect, archiepiscopal. In Biol. and Anat. it usually means primitive, original, ancestral; as, archipterygium, the primitive fin or wing.

architecture.etymology: L. architectura, fr. architectus: cf. F. architecture. See Architect.

architrave.etymology: F. architrave, fr. It. architrave; pref. archi- + trave beam, L. trabs.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying chief, arch; as, architect, archiepiscopal. In Biol. and Anat. it usually means primitive, original, ancestral; as, archipterygium, the primitive fin or wing.

archive.etymology: F. archives, pl., L. archivum, archium, fr. Gr. Archi-, pref.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying chief, arch; as, architect, archiepiscopal. In Biol. and Anat. it usually means primitive, original, ancestral; as, archipterygium, the primitive fin or wing.

arcuate.etymology: L. arcuatus, p. p. of arcuare to shape like a bow, fr. arcus. See Arc.

ardent.etymology: OE. ardaunt, F. ardant, p. pr. of arder to burn, fr. L. ardere.

ardor.etymology: L. ardor, fr. ardere to burn: cf. OF. ardor, ardur, F. ardeur.

arduous.etymology: L. arduus steep, high; akin to Ir. ard high, height.

are.etymology: AS. (Northumbrian) aron, akin to the 1st pers. pl. forms, Icel. erum, Goth. sijum, L. sumus, Gr. smas; all from a root as. Am and Is, and cf. Be.

area.etymology: L. area a broad piece of level groAre, n.

areca.etymology: Canarese adiki: cf. Pg. & Sp. areca.

arena.etymology: L. arena, harena, sand, a sandy place.

areola.etymology: L. areola, dim. of area: cf. F. aréole. See Area.

arete.etymology: F., lit., a sharp fish bone, ridge, sharp edge, fr. L. arista beard of grain.

argent.etymology: F. argent, fr. L. argentum, silver; akin to Gr. rajata white, silver, raj to shine, Ir. arg white, milk, airgiod silver, money, and L. arguere to make clear. See Argue.

argentiferous.etymology: L. argentum silver + -ferous: cf. F. argentifère.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

argentine.etymology: Cf. F. argentin, fr. L. argentum silver.

argil.etymology: F. argile, L. argilla white clay, akin to Gr. Argent.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

argosy.etymology: Earlier ragusy, fr. ragusa meaning orig. a vessel of Ragusa.

argue.etymology: OE. arguen, F. arguer, fr. L. argutare, freq. of arguere to make clear; from the same root as E. argent.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

argument.etymology: From Middle English argument , from Anglo-Norman and Old French arguement , from Latin argumentum . The English word is analysable as argue +‎ -ment . Doublet of argumentum .

argumentation.etymology: L. argumentatio, from argumentari: cf. F. argumentation.

aria.etymology: It., fr. L. aër. See Air.

arid.etymology: L. aridus, fr. arere to be dry: cf. F. aride.

arietta.etymology: It. arietta, dim. of aria; F. ariette.

aril.etymology: From LL. arilli dry grapes, perh. fr. L. aridus dry: cf. F,. arille.

arise.etymology: AS. arisan; a (equiv. to Goth. us-, ur-, G. er-, orig. meaning out) + risan to rise; cf. Goth. urreisan to arise. See Rise.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting divination; as, aleuromancy, chiromancy, necromancy, etc.

arithmetic.etymology: OE. arsmetike, OF. arismetique, L. arithmetica, fr. Gr. arm, the idea of counting coming from that of fitting, attaching. See Arm. The modern Eng. and French forms are accommodated to the Greek.

arles.etymology: Cf. F. arrhes, Scot. airles. Cf. Earles penny.

arm.etymology: AS. arm, earm; akin to OHG. aram, G., D., Dan., & Sw. arm, Icel. armr, Goth. arms, L. armus arm, shoulder, and prob. to Gr. rame. Art, Article.

armada.etymology: Sp. armada, L. as if armata (sc. classic fleet), fr. armatus, p. p. of armare. See Arm, v. t. Army.

armadillo.etymology: Sp. armadillo, dim. of armado armed, p. p. of armar to arm. Do called from being armed with a bony shell.

armament.etymology: L. armamenta, pl., utensils, esp. the tackle of a ship, fr. armare to arm: cf. LL. armamentum, F. armement.

armature.etymology: L. armatura, fr. armare to arm: cf. F. armature. See Arm, v. t., Armor.

armenian.etymology: Cf. F. Arménien, L. Armenias, fr. Armenia.

armet.etymology: F., dim. of arme arm, or corrupted for healmet helmet.

armiger.etymology: L. armiger armor bearer; arma arms + gerere to bear.

armillary.etymology: LL. armillarius, fr. L. armilla arm ring, bracelet, fr. armus arm: cf. F. armillaire. See Arm, n.

armistice.etymology: F. armistice, fr. (an assumed word) L. armistitium; arma arms + stare, statum (combining form, -stitum), to stand still.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix having a diminutive force; as in streamlet, armlet.

armor.etymology: OE. armure, fr. F. armure, OF. armeure, fr. L. armatura. See Armature.

armorer.etymology: OE. armurer, armerer, fr. F. armurter, fr. armure armor.

armorial.etymology: F. armorial, fr. armoiries arms, coats of arms, for armoieries, fr. OF. armoier to paint arms, coats of arms, fr. armes, fr. L. arma. See Arms, Armory.

armory.etymology: OF. armaire, armarie, F. armoire, fr. L. armarium place for keeping arms; but confused with F. armoiries. See Armorial, Ambry.

arms.etymology: OE. armes, F. arme, pl. armes, fr. L. arma, pl., arms, orig. fittings, akin to armus shoulder, and E. arm. See Arm, n.

army.etymology: F. armée, fr. L. armata, fem. of armatus, p. p. of armare to arm. Cf. Armada.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

aroma.etymology: L. aroma, Gr. aromaz, aromat, spice, F. aromate.

aromatic.etymology: L. aromaticus, Gr. aromatique. See Aroma.

arpeggio.etymology: It., fr. arpeggiare to play on the harp, fr. arpa harp.

arpent.etymology: F. arpent, fr. L. arepennis, arapennis. According to Columella, a Gallic word for a measure equiv. to half a Roman jugerum.

arquebus.etymology: F. arquebuse, OF. harquebuse, fr. D. haak-bus; cf. G. hakenbüchse a gun with a hook. See Hagbut.

arrack.etymology: Ar. araq sweat, juice, spirituous liquor, fr. araqa to sweat. Cf. Rack arrack.

arraign.etymology: OE. arainen, arenen, OF. aragnier, aranier, araisnier, F. arraisonner, fr. LL. arrationare to address to call before court; L. ad + ratio reason, reasoning, LL. cause, judgment. See Reason.

arrange.etymology: OE. arayngen, OF. arengier, F. arranger, fr. a (L. ad) + OF. rengier, rangier, F. ranger. See Range, v. t.

arrant.etymology: OE. erraunt, errant, errand, equiv. to E. errant wandering, which was first applied to vagabonds, as an errant rogue, an errant thief, and hence passed gradually into its present and worse sense. See Errant.

arras.etymology: From Arras the capital of Artois, in the French Netherlands.

array.etymology: OE. arai, arrai, OF. arrai, arrei, arroi, order, arrangement, dress, F. arroi; a (L. ad) + OF. rai, rei, roi, order, arrangement, fr. G. or Scand.; cf. Goth. raidjan, garaidjan, to arrange, MHG. gereiten, Icel. reithi rigging, harness; akin to E. ready. Cf. Ready, Greith, Curry.

arrest.etymology: OE. aresten, OF. arester, F. arrêter, fr. LL. arrestare; L. ad + restare to remain, stop; re + stare to stand. See Rest remainder.

arrive.etymology: OE. ariven to arrive, land, OF. ariver, F. arriver, fr. LL. arripare, adripare, to come to shore; L. ad + ripa the shore or sloping bank of a river. Cf. Riparian.

arroba.etymology: Sp. and Pg., from Ar. arrub, ar-rubu, a fourth part.

arrogance.etymology: F., fr. L. arrogantia, fr. arrogans. See Arrogant.

arrogant.etymology: F. arrogant, L. arrogans, p. pr. of arrogare. See Arrogate.

arrogate.etymology: L. arrogatus, p. p. of adrogare, arrogare, to ask, appropriate to one's self; ad + rogare to ask. See Rogation.

arrogation.etymology: L. arrogatio, fr. arrogare. Cf. Adrogation.

arrow.etymology: OE. arewe, AS. arewe, earh; akin to Icel. ör, örvar, Goth. arhwazna, and perh. L. arcus bow. Cf. Arc.

arsenal.etymology: Sp. & F. arsenal arsenal, dockyard, or It. arzanale, arsenale (cf. It. & darsena dock); all fr. Ar. dar house of industry or fabrication; dar house + art, industry.

arsenic.etymology: L. arsenicum, Gr. zernikh: cf. F. arsenic.

arson.etymology: OF. arson, arsun, fr. L. ardere, arsum, to burn.

art.etymology: F. art, L. ars, artis, orig., skill in joining or fitting; prob. akin to E. arm, aristocrat, article.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

arteriole.etymology: NL. arteriola, dim. of L. arteria: cf. F. artériole.

artesian.etymology: F. artésien, fr. Artois in France, where many such wells have been made since the middle of the last century.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.
A combining form meaning part, portion; as, blastomere, epimere.
A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.

artichoke.etymology: It. articioc, perh. corrupted fr. the same word as carciofo; cf. older spellings archiciocco, archicioffo, carciocco, and Sp. alcachofa, Pg. alcachofra; prob. fr. Ar. al- harshaf, al-kharsh.

roots.meaning: All; wholly; completely; as, almighty,almost. (b) Etym: [L. ad.]

article.etymology: F., fr. L. articulus, dim. of artus joint, akin to Gr. ar to join, fit. See Art, n.

articular.etymology: L. articularis: cf. F. articulaire. See Article, n.

articulation.etymology: Cf. F. articulation, fr. L. articulatio.

artifact.etymology: L. ars, artis, art + facere, factum, to make.

artifice.etymology: L. artificium, fr. artifex artificer; ars, artis, art + facere to make: cf. F. artifice.

artificer.etymology: Cf. F. artificier, fr. LL. artificiarius.

artificial.etymology: L. artificialis, fr. artificium: cf. F. artificiel. See Artifice.

artillery.etymology: OE. artilrie, OF. artillerie, arteillerie, fr. LL. artillaria, artilleria, machines and apparatus of all kinds used in war, vans laden with arms of any kind which follow camps; F. artillerie great guns, ordnance; OF. artillier to work artifice, to fortify, to arm, prob. from L. ars, artis, skill in joining something, art. See Art.

artisan.etymology: F. artisan, fr. L. artitus skilled in arts, fr. ars, artis, art: cf. It. artigiano. See Art, n.

artist.etymology: F. artiste, LL. artista, fr. L. ars. See Art, n., and cf. Artiste.

aryan.etymology: Skr. arya excellent, honorable; akin to the name of the country Iran, and perh. to Erin, Ireland, and the early name of this people, at least in Asia.

asarabacca.etymology: L. asarum + bacca a berry. See Asarone.

ascend.etymology: L. ascendere; ad + scandere to climb, mount. See Scan.

ascendant.etymology: F. ascendant, L. ascendens; p. pr. of ascendere.

ascension.etymology: F. ascension, L. ascensio, fr. ascendere. See Ascend.

ascent.etymology: Formed like descent, as if from a F. ascente, fr. a verb ascendre, fr. L. ascendere. See Ascend, Descent.

ascertain.etymology: OF. acertener; a (L. ad) + certain. See Certain.

asclepias.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Asclepios or Aesculapius.

ascribe.etymology: L. ascribere, adscribere, to ascribe; ad + scribere to write: cf. OF. ascrire. See Scribe.

ascription.etymology: L. ascriptio, fr. ascribere. See Ascribe.

ash.etymology: OE. asch, esh, AS. æsc; akin to OHG. asc, Sw. & Dan. ask, Icel. askr, D. esch, G. esche.

ashamed.etymology: Orig. a p. p. of ashame, v. t.

ashlar.etymology: OE. ascheler, achiler, OF. aiseler, fr. aiselle, dim. of ais plank, fr. L. axis, assis, plank, axle. See Axle.

asinine.etymology: L. asininus, fr. asinus ass. See Ass.

ask.etymology: OE. asken, ashen, axien, AS. ascian, acsian; akin to OS. escon, OHG. eiscon, Sw. aska, Dan. æske, D. eischen, G. heischen, Lith. jëskóti, OSlav. iskati to seek, Skr. ish to desire. *5.

askance.etymology: Cf. D. schuin, schuins, sideways, schuiven to shove, schuinte slope. Cf. Asquint.

askant.etymology: Cf. D. schuin, schuins, sideways, schuiven to shove, schuinte slope. Cf. Asquint.

asker.etymology: A corruption of AS. a lizard, newt.

asp.etymology: L. aspis, fr. Gr. aspe, F. aspic.

asparagus.etymology: L., fr. Gr. prong, sprout, Pers. asparag, Lith. spurgas sprout, Skr. sphurj to swell. Perh. the Greek borrowed from the Persian. Cf. Sparrowgrass.

aspect.etymology: L. aspectus, fr. aspicere, aspectum, to look at; ad + spicere, specere, to look, akin to E. spy.

aspen.etymology: AS. æsp, æps; akin to OHG. aspa, Icel. ösp, Dan. æsp, Sw. asp, D. esp, G. espe, äspe, aspe; cf. Lettish apsa, Lith. apuszis.

asper.etymology: OE. aspre, OF. aspre, F. âpre, fr. L. asper rough.

aspergill.etymology: LL. aspergillum, fr. L. aspergere. See Asperse, v. t.

asperity.etymology: L. asperitas, fr. asper rough: cf. F. aspérité.

asperse.etymology: L. aspersus, p. p. of aspergere to scatter, sprinkle; ad + spargere to strew. See Sparse.

aspersion.etymology: L. aspersio, fr. aspergere: cf. F. aspersion.

aspirant.etymology: Cf. F. aspirant, p. pr. of aspirer. See Aspire.

aspirate.etymology: L. aspiratus, p. p. of aspirare to breathe toward or upon, to add the breathing h; ad + spirare to breathe, blow. Cf. Aspire.

aspiration.etymology: L. aspiratio, fr. aspirare: cf. F. aspiration.

aspire.etymology: F. aspirer, L. aspirare. See Aspirate, v. t.

ass.etymology: OE. asse, AS. assa; akin to Icel. asni, W. asen, asyn, L. asinus, dim. aselus, Gr. esol, OHG. esil, G. esel, Goth. asilus, Dan. æsel, Lith. asilas, Bohem. osel, Pol. osiel. The word is prob. of Semitic origin; cf. Heb. ath she ass. Cf. Ease.

assagai.etymology: Pg. azagaia, Sp. azagaya, fr. a Berber word. Cf. Lancegay.

assail.etymology: OE. assailen, asailen, OF. asaillir, assailler, F. assaillir; (L. ad) + saillir to burst out, project, fr. L. salire to leap, spring; cf. L. assilire to leap or spring upon. See Sally.

assailant.etymology: F. assaillant, p. pr. of assaillir.

assassin.etymology: F. (cf. It. assassino), fr. Ar. one who has drunk of the hashish. Under its influence the Assassins of the East, followers of the Shaikh al-Jabal (Old Man of the Mountain), were said to commit the murders required by their chief.

assassinate.etymology: LL. assassinatus, p. p. of assassinare.

assault.etymology: OE. asaut, assaut, OF. assaut, asalt, F. assaut, LL. assaltus; L. ad + saltus a leaping, a springing, salire to leap. See Assail.

assay.etymology: OF. asai, essai, trial, F. essa. See Essay, n.

assegai.etymology: Pg. azagaia, Sp. azagaya, fr. a Berber word. Cf. Lancegay.

assemble.etymology: F. assembler, fr. LL. assimulare to bring together to collect; L. ad + simul together; akin to similis like, Gr. same. Cf. Assimilate, Same.

assembly.etymology: F. assemblée, fr. assembler. See Assemble.

assent.etymology: F. assentir, L. assentire, assentiri; ad + sentire to feel, think. See Sense.

assert.etymology: L. assertus, p. p. of asserere to join or fasten to one's self, claim, maintain; ad + serere to join or bind together. See Series.

assess.etymology: OF. assesser to regulate, settle, LL. assessare to value for taxation, fr. L. assidere, supine as if assessum, to sit by, esp. of judges in a court, in LL. to assess, tax. Cf. Assize, v., Cess.

assessor.etymology: L., one who sits beside, the assistant of a judge, fr. assid. See Assession. LL., one who arranges of determines the taxes, fr. assid. See Assess, v., and cf. Cessor.

assets.etymology: OF. asez enough, F. assez, fr. L. ad + satis, akin to Gr. saps full. Cf. Assai, Satisfy.

asseverate.etymology: L. asseveratus, p. p. of asseverare to assert seriously or earnestly; ad + severus. See Severe.

assibilate.etymology: L. assibilatus, p. p. of assibilare to hiss out; ad + sibilare to hiss.

assiduity.etymology: L. assiduitas: cf. F. assiduite. See Assiduous.

assiduous.etymology: L. assiduus, fr. assid to sit near or close; ad + sed to sit. See Sit.

assign.etymology: OE. assignen, asignen, F. assigner, fr. L. assignare; ad + signare to mark, mark out, designate, signum mark, sign. See Sign.

assignation.etymology: L. assignatio, fr. assignare: cf. F. assignation.

assignee.etymology: F. assigné, p. p. of assigner. See Assign, v., and cf. Assign an assignee.

assimilate.etymology: L. assimilatus, p. p. of assimilare; ad + similare to make like, similis like. See Similar, Assemble, Assimilate.

assist.etymology: L. assistere; ad + sistere to cause to stand, to stand, from stare to stand: cf. F. assister. See Stand.

assistant.etymology: Cf. F. assistant, p. pr. of assister.

assize.etymology: OE. assise, asise, OF. assise, F. assises, assembly of judges, the decree pronounced by them, tax, impost, fr. assis, assise, p. p. of asseoir, fr. L. assid to sit by; ad + sed to sit. See Sit, Size, and cf. Excise, Assess.

associate.etymology: L. associatus, p. p. of associare; ad + sociare to join or unite, socius companion. See Social.

association.etymology: Cf. F. association, LL. associatio, fr. L. associare.

assoil.etymology: OF. assoiler, absoiler, assoldre, F. absoudre, L. absolvere. See Absolve.

assonant.etymology: L. assonans, p. pr. of assonare to sound to, to correspond to in sound; ad + sonare to sound, sonus sound: cf. F. assonant. See Sound.

assonate.etymology: L. assonare, assonatum, to respond to.

assort.etymology: F. assortir; (L. ad) + sortir to cast or draw lots, to obtain by lot, L. sortiri, fr. sors, sortis, lot. See Sort.

assuage.etymology: OE. asuagen, aswagen, OF. asoagier, asuagier, fr. assouagier, fr. L. ad + suavis sweet. See Sweet.

assuasive.etymology: From assuage, as if this were fr. a supposed L. assuadere to persuade to; or from E. pref. ad + -suasive as in persuasive.

assume.etymology: L. assumere; ad + sumere to take; sub + emere to take, buy: cf. F. assumer. See Redeem.

assumption.etymology: OE. assumpcioun a taking up into heaven, L. assumptio a taking, fr. assumere: cf. F. assomption. See Assume.

assumptive.etymology: L. assumptivus, fr. assumptus, fr. assumere.

assurance.etymology: OE. assuraunce, F. assurance, fr. assurer. See Assure.

assure.etymology: OF. aseürer, F. assurer, LL. assecurare; L. ad + securus secure, sure, certain. See Secure, Sure, and cf. Insure.

assurgent.etymology: L. assurgens, p. pr. of assurgere; ad + surgere to rise.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

aster.etymology: L. aster aster, star, Gr. Star.

asthma.etymology: Gr. va, Goth. waian, to blow, E. wind.

astonish.etymology: OE. astonien, astunian, astonen, OF. estoner, F. étonner, fr. L. ex out + tonare to thunder, but perhaps influenced by E. stun. See Thunder, Astound, Astony.

astound.etymology: OE. astouned, astound, astoned, p. p. of astone. See Astone.

astral.etymology: L. astralis, fr. astrum star, Gr. astral. See Star.

astringe.etymology: L. astringere; ad + stringere to draw tight. Cf. Astrict, and see Strain, v. t.

astringent.etymology: L. astringens, p. pr. of astringere: cf. F. astringent. See Astringe.

roots.meaning: The combining form of the Greek word 'a`stron, meaning star.

astrology.etymology: F. astrologie, L. astrologia, fr. Gr. Star.

roots.meaning: The combining form of the Greek word 'a`stron, meaning star.

astronomy.etymology: OE. astronomie, F. astronomie, L. astronomia, fr. Gr. Star, and Nomad.

roots.meaning: The combining form of the Greek word 'a`stron, meaning star.

astute.etymology: L. astutus, fr. astus craft, cunning; perh. cognate with E. acute.

atavism.etymology: L. atavus an ancestor, fr. avus a grandfather.

athanor.etymology: F., fr. Ar. at-tannur, fr. Heb. tannur an oven or furnace.

athenaeum.etymology: L. Athenaemum, Gr. Minerva by the Romans), the tutelary goddess of Athens.

atheneum.etymology: L. Athenaemum, Gr. Minerva by the Romans), the tutelary goddess of Athens.

athirst.etymology: OE. ofthurst, AS. ofpyrsted, p. p. of ofpyrstan; pref. of-, intensive + pyrstan to thirst. See Thirst.

athlete.etymology: L. athleta, Gr. wed: cf. F. athlète.

atlantic.etymology: L. Atlanticus, fr. Atlas. See Atlas and Atlantes.

atlas.etymology: L. Atlas, -antis, Gr. Atlas, in W. Africa, regarded as the pillar of heaven. It is from the root of Tolerate.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

atmosphere.etymology: Gr. atman breath, soul, G. athem breath) + atmosphère. See Sphere.

atoll.etymology: The native name in the Indian Ocean.

atom.etymology: L. atomus, Gr. atome. See Tome.

atrium.etymology: L., the fore court of a Roman house.

atrocious.etymology: L. atrox, atrocis, cruel, fierce: cf. F. atroce.

atrocity.etymology: F. atrocité, L. atrocitas, fr. atrox, atrocis, cruel.

attach.etymology: OF. atachier, F. attacher, to tie or fasten: cf. Celt. tac, tach, nail, E. tack a small nail, tack to fasten. Cf. Attack, and see Tack.

attache.etymology: F., p. p. of attacher. See Attach, v. t.

attack.etymology: F. attaquer, orig. another form of attacher to attack: cf. It. attacare to fasten, attack. See Attach, Tack a small nail.

attain.etymology: Of. atteinen, atteignen, , OF. ateindre, ataindre, F. atteindre, fr. L. attingere; ad + tangere to touch, reach. See Tangent, and cf. Attinge, Attaint.

attainder.etymology: OF. ataindre, ateindre, to accuse, convict. Attainder is often erroneously referred to F. teindre tie stain. See Attaint, Attain.

attaint.etymology: OE. atteynten to convict, fr. atteynt, OF. ateint, p. p. of ateindre, ataindre. The meanings 3, 4, 5, and 6 were influenced by a supposed connection with taint. See Attain, Attainder.

attar.etymology: Per. 'atar perfume, essence, Ar. 'itr, fr. 'atara to smell sweet. Cf. Otto.

attemper.etymology: OF. atemprer, fr. L. attemperare; ad + temperare to soften, temper. See Temper, and cf. Attemperate.

attempt.etymology: OF. atenter, also spelt atempter, F. attenter, fr. L. attentare to attempt; ad + tentare, temptare, to touch, try, v. intens. of tendere to stretch. See Tempt, and cf. Attend.

attend.etymology: OE. atenden, OF. atendre, F. attendre, to expect, to wait, fr. L. attendre to stretch, (sc. animum), to apply the mind to; ad + tendere to stretch. See Tend.

attendance.etymology: OE. attendance, OF. atendance, fr. atendre, F. attendre. See Attend, v. t.

attendant.etymology: F. attendant, p. pr. of attendre. See Attend, v. t.

attenuate.etymology: L. attenuatus, p. p. of attenuare; ad + tenuare to make thin, tenuis thin. See Thin.

attest.etymology: L. attestari; ad + testari to bear witness: cf. F. attester.

attic.etymology: In sense (a) from F. attique, orig. meaning Attic. See Attic, a.

attire.etymology: OE. atiren to array, dispose, arrange, OF. atirier; à (L. ad) + F. tire rank, order, row; of Ger. origin: cf. As. tier row, OHG. ziari, G. zier, ornament, zieren to adorn. Cf. Tire a headdress.

attitude.etymology: It. attitudine, LL. aptitudo, fr. L. aptus suited, fitted: cf. F. attitude. Cf. Aptitude.

attorn.etymology: OF. atorner, aturner, atourner, to direct, prepare, dispose, attorn (cf. OE. atornen to return, adorn); à (L. ad) + torner to turn; cf. LL. attornare to commit business to another, to attorn; ad + tornare to turn, L. tornare to turn in a lathe, to round off. See Turn, v. t.

attorney.etymology: OE. aturneye, OF. atorné, p. p. of atorner: cf. LL. atturnatus, attornatus, fr. attornare. See Attorn.

attract.etymology: L. attractus, p. p. of attrahere; ad + trahere to draw. See Trace, v. t.

attribute.etymology: L. attributus, p. p. of attribuere; ad + tribuere to bestow. See Tribute.

roots.meaning: As a prefix ad- assumes the forms ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, assimilating the d with the first letter of the word to which ad- is prefixed. It remains unchanged before vowels, and before d, h, j, m, v. Examples: adduce, adhere, adjacent, admit, advent, accord, affect, aggregate, allude, annex, appear, etc. It becomes ac- before qu, as in acquiesce.

auburn.etymology: OE. auburne blonde, OF. alborne, auborne, fr. LL. alburnus whitish, fr. L. albus white. Cf. Alburn.

auction.etymology: L. auctio an increasing, a public sale, where the price was called out, and the article to be sold was adjudged to the last increaser of the price, or the highest bidder, fr. L. augere, auctum, to increase. See Augment.

audacious.etymology: F. audacieux, as if fr. LL. audaciosus (not found), fr. L. audacia audacity, fr. audax, -acis, bold, fr. audere to dare.

audible.etymology: LL. audibilis, fr. L. audire, auditum, to hear: cf. Gr. auris, and E. ear.

audience.etymology: F. audience, L. audientia, fr. audire to hear. See Audible, a.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

audit.etymology: L. auditus a hearing, fr. audire. See Audible, a.

auditor.etymology: L. auditor, fr. audire. See Audible, a.

auger.etymology: OE. augoure, nauger, AS. nafegar, fr. nafu, nafa, nave of a wheel + gar spear, and therefore meaning properly and originally a nave-bore. See Nave (of a wheel) and 2d Gore, n.

aught.etymology: AS. , fr. agan to own, p. p. ahte.

augment.etymology: L. augmentare, fr. augmentum an increase, fr. augere to increase; perh. akin to Gr. wax, v., and eke, v.: cf. F. augmenter.

augur.etymology: L. Of uncertain origin: the first part of the word is perh. fr. L. avis bird, and the last syllable, gur, equiv. to the Skr. gar to call, akin to L. garrulus garrulous.

august.etymology: L. augustus; cf. augere to increase; in the language of religion, to honor by offerings: cf. F. auguste. See Augment.

augustan.etymology: L. Augustanus, fr. Augustus. See August, n.

auk.etymology: Prov. E. alk; akin to Dan. alke, Icel. & Sw. alka.

aunt.etymology: OF. ante, F. tante, L. amita father's sister. Cf. Amma.

aureate.etymology: L. aureatus, fr. aureus golden, fr. aurum gold.

aureole.etymology: F. auréole, fr. L. aureola, (fem adj.) of gold (sc. corona crown), dim. of aureus. See Aureate, Oriole.

auricle.etymology: L. auricula, dim. of auris ear. See Ear.

auricular.etymology: LL. auricularis: cf. F. auriculaire. See Auricle.

auriferous.etymology: L. aurifer; aurum gold + ferre to bear: cf. F. aurifère.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

aurochs.etymology: G. auerochs, OHG. ; (cf. AS. ) + ohso ox, G. ochs. Cf. Owre, Ox.

aurora.etymology: L. aurora, for ausosa, akin to Gr. ushas, and E. east.

auscultation.etymology: L. ausculcatio, fr. auscultare to listen, fr. a dim. of auris, orig. ausis, ear. See Auricle, and cf. Scout, n.

auspicate.etymology: L. auspicatus, p. p. of auspicari to take auspices, fr. auspex a bird seer, an augur, a contr. of avispex; avis bird + specere, spicere, to view. See Aviary, Spy.

auspice.etymology: L. auspicium, fr. auspex: cf. F. auspice. See Auspicate, a.

austere.etymology: F. austère, L. austerus, fr. Gr. Sear.

austerity.etymology: F. austérité, L. austerias, fr. austerus. See Austere.

austral.etymology: L. australis, fr. auster: cf. F. austral.

australian.etymology: From L. Terra Australis southern land.

authentic.etymology: OE. autentik, OF. autentique, F. authentique, L. authenticus coming from the real author, of original or firsthand authority, from Gr. sons and perh. orig. from the p. pr. of to be, root as, and meaning the one it really is. See Am, Sin, n., and cf. Effendi.

author.etymology: OE. authour, autour, OF. autor, F. auteur, fr. L. auctor, sometimes, but erroneously, written autor or author, fr. augere to increase, to produce. See Auction, n.

authority.etymology: OE. autorite, auctorite, F. autorité, fr. L. auctoritas, fr. auctor. See Author, n.

authorize.etymology: OE. autorize, F. autoriser, fr. LL. auctorizare, authorisare. See Author.

automaton.etymology: L. fr. Gr. ma, man, to strive, think, cf. Mean, v. i.

autumn.etymology: L. auctumnus, autumnus, perh. fr. a root av to satisfy one's self: cf. F. automne. See Avarice.

autumnal.etymology: L. auctumnalis, autumnalis: cf. F. automnal.

auxiliary.etymology: L. auxiliarius, fr. auxilium help, aid, fr. augere to increase.

avail.etymology: OE. availen, fr. F. ad) + valoir to be worth, fr. L. valere to be strong, to be worth. See Valiant.

available.etymology: From Middle English available , avayllable , avayleable , equivalent of avail +‎ -able .

avalanche.etymology: F. avalanche, fr. avaler to descend, to let down, from aval down, downward; ad) + val, L. vallis, valley. See Valley.

avarice.etymology: F. avaritia, fr. avarus avaricious, prob. fr. av to covert, fr. a root av to satiate one's self: cf. Gr. av to satiate one's self, rejoice, protect.

avatar.etymology: Skr. avatâra descent; ava from + root t to cross, pass over.

avellane.etymology: Cf. It. avellana a filbert, fr. L. Avella or Abella a city of Campania.

avenge.etymology: OF. avengier; L. ad + vindicare to lay claim to, to avenge, revenge. See Vengeance.

avenue.etymology: F. avenue, fr. avenir to come to, L. advenire. See Advene.

aver.etymology: OF. aver domestic animal, whence LL. averia, pl. cattle. See Habit, and cf. Average.

average.etymology: OF. average, LL. averagium, prob. fr. OF. aver, F. avoir, property, horses, cattle, etc.; prop. infin., to have, from L. habere to have. Cf. F. avérage small cattle, and avarie (perh. of different origin) damage to ship or cargo, port dues. The first meaning was peAver, n., Avercorn, Averpenny.

averment.etymology: Cf. OF. averement, LL. averamentum. See Aver, v. t.

averse.etymology: L. aversus, p. p. of avertere. See Avert.

aversion.etymology: L. aversio: cf. F. aversion. See Avert.

avert.etymology: L. avertere; a, ab + vertere to turn: cf. OF. avertir. See Verse, n.

aviary.etymology: L. aviarium, fr. aviarius pertaining to birds, fr. avis bird, akin to Gr, vi.

avid.etymology: L. avidus, fr. av to long: cf. F. avide. See Avarice.

avidity.etymology: L. aviditas, fr. avidus: cf. F. avidité. See Avid.

avifauna.etymology: NL., fr. L. avis bird + E. fauna.

avocado.etymology: Corrupted from the Mexican ahuacatl: cf. Sp. aguacate, F. aguacaté, avocat, G. avogadobaum.

avocet.etymology: F. avocette: cf. It. avosetta, Sp. avoceta.

avoid.etymology: OF. esvuidier, es (L. ex) + vuidier, voidier, to empty. See Void, a.

avoirdupois.etymology: OE. aver de peis, goods of weight, where peis is fr. OF. peis weight, F. poids, L. pensum. See Aver, n., and Poise, n.

avouch.etymology: OF. avochier, LL. advocare to recognize the existence of a thing, to advocate, fr. L. advocare to call to; ad + vocare to call. Cf. Avow to declare, Advocate, and see Vouch, v. t.

avow.etymology: F. avouver, fr. L. advocare to call to (whence the meanings, to call upon as superior; recognize as lord, own, confess); ad + vocare to call. See Advocate, Avouch.

avulse.etymology: L. avulsus, p. p. of avellere to tear off; a (ab) + vellere to pluck.

await.etymology: OF. awaitier, agaitier; (L. ad) + waitier, gaitier to watch, F. guetter. See Wait.

awake.etymology: AS. awæcnan, v. i. (imp. aw), and awacian, v. i. (imp. awacode). See Awaken, Wake.

awaken.etymology: OE. awakenen, awaknen, AS. awæcnan, awæcnian, v. i.; pref. on- + wæcnan to wake. Cf. Awake, v. t.

award.etymology: OF. eswarder to look at, consider, decide, judge; es (L. ex) + warder, garder, to observe, take heed, keep, fr. OHG. wart to watch, guard. See Ward.

aware.etymology: OE. iwar, AS. gewær, fr. wær wary. The pref. ge- orig. meant together, completely. Wary.

roots.meaning: An Anglo-Saxon prefix. See Y-.

away.etymology: AS. aweg, anweg, onweg; on on + weg way.

awe.etymology: OE. a, aghe, fr. Icel. agi; akin to AS. ege, , Goth. agis, Dan. ave chastisement, fear, Gr. ail. Ugly.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

awl.etymology: OE. aul, awel, al, AS. , awel; akin to Icel. alr, OHG. ala, G. ahle, Lith. yla, Skr. ara.

awning.etymology: Origin uncertain: cf. F. auvent awing, or Pers. awan, awang, anything suspended, or LG. havening a place sheltered from wind and weather, E. haven.

axe.etymology: OE. ax, axe, AS. eax, æx, acas; akin to D. akse, OS. accus, OHG. acchus, G. axt, Icel. öx, öxi, Sw. yxe, Dan. ökse, Goth. aqizi, Gr. , L. ascia; not akin to E. acute.

axiom.etymology: L. axioma, Gr. that which is thought worthy, that which is assumed, a basis of demonstration, a principle, fr. to think worthy, fr. worthy, weighing as much as; cf. to lead, drive, also to weigh so much: cf F. axiome. See Agent, a.

axle.etymology: OE. axel, exel, shoulder, AS. ; akin to AS. eax axle, Sw. & Dan. axel shoulder, ~, G. achse axle, achsel shoulder, L. axis axle, Gr. aksha, L. axilla shoulder joint: cf. F. essieu, axle, OF. aissel, fr. dim. of L. axis. Axis.

ayah.etymology: Pg. aia, akin to Sp. aya a governess, ayo a tutor.

azedarach.etymology: F. azédarac, Sp. acederaque, Pers. azaddirakht noble tree.

azimuth.etymology: OE. azimut, F. azimut, fr. Ar. as-sum, pl. of as-samt a way, or perh., a point of the horizon and a circle extending to it from the zenith, as being the Arabic article: cf. It. azzimutto, Pg. azimuth, and Ar. samt-al-ra's the vertex of the heaven. Cf. Zenith.

azure.etymology: F. & OSp. azur, Sp. azul, through Ar. from Per. lajaward, or lajuward, lapis lazuli, a blue color, lajawardi, lajuwardi, azure, cerulean, the initial l having been dropped, perhaps by the influence of the Ar. azr-aq azure, blue. Cf. G. lasur, lasurstein, azure color, azure stone, and NL. lapis lazuli.
